VERDICT: DISPLACEMENT
CONFIDENCE: LOW
CONFIDENCE_BASIS: Corroborating — exposed_vs_control_jobs (exposed -1.27% YoY vs control +1.27%, differential -2.54, +2.08 SD past the clean pre-2020 window and parked past its -2.48 line, as_of 2026-06), reabsorption headline (prime-age employment share 80.2, 12m change -0.5 at +1.77 SD, decomposition shows employment itself down -1.38%, as_of 2026-06) plus its long-term-unemployed readout (27.3%, +4.0 in 12m), with ai_adoption (21.7% of firms and rising, 38.8% at 250+ employees, as_of 2026-07) opening the deployment gate; failing to corroborate or refuting — job_postings_spread (6-month change +2.6, i.e. the earliest and occupation-cut panel is easing, as_of 2026-07), reabsorption's own layoffs_rate (1.1, -0.1 over 12m, below norm: frozen not shedding) and hires_minus_quits (1.4, +0.1 over 12m), exposed_vs_control_wages (+1.11 in favour of exposed, though its own weighting rule disqualifies it while exposed employment falls), labor_productivity (2.8%, in the internet-boom band, as_of 2026-03); all three doubts are unmet — the entire 12-month EPOP decline sits inside the last 3 months (3m change also -0.5), the independent establishment source is economy-wide positive (+57k payrolls, 4.2% unemployment) against the household survey's fall, and the leading postings panel is pointing the other way.
LOAD_BEARING_PANELS: reabsorption, exposed_vs_control_jobs, ai_adoption
CONFOUNDER: NONE
OVERTURN_PANEL: reabsorption
OVERTURN_FIELD: headline.change_over_12_months
OVERTURN_COMPARATOR: at_or_above
OVERTURN_VALUE: 0.0
OVERTURN_UNIT: percentage points (12-month change in the 25-54 employment-population ratio)
OVERTURN_ALSO_PANEL: reabsorption
OVERTURN_ALSO_FIELD: secondary.long_term_unemployed_share.latest_value
OVERTURN_ALSO_COMPARATOR: at_or_below
OVERTURN_ALSO_VALUE: 25.0
OVERTURN_BY: 2026-11-02
OVERTURN_PLAIN: The prime-age employment-share chart moves first: if it climbs back to flat or better year-over-year while the long-term-unemployed share falls back to 25% or less, the aggregate market is catching exits again and this displacement reading was wrong.

REASONING_LOG:

**What I am claiming, plainly.** This is not "displacement not started" being dressed up, and it is not resting on absence of deterioration. It rests on observed deterioration: the household survey's prime-age employment share is down 0.5 points over twelve months at +1.77 SD against the clean pre-2020 window, past this panel's own registered 1-SD deterioration line, and the decomposition says employment itself is down 1.4 million (-1.38%) rather than the population having grown. Paired with an exposed-industry job growth rate that is outright negative (-1.27% YoY) while controls run +1.27%, that is the combination the dashboard's own logic reserves for displacement rather than reallocation: something specific to exposed work, and the aggregate has not caught the outflow. The confidence is LOW because almost all of the absorption movement is one quarter old, the leading panel is improving, and the establishment survey disagrees with the household survey economy-wide.

**exposed_vs_control_jobs (ATTRIBUTION, as_of 2026-06, 2 months old).** Name the sides: exposed industries are contracting at -1.27% YoY; controls are expanding at +1.27%. The differential -2.54 sits past the -2.48 attribution line and +2.08 SD past the fixed 2010-2019 window (I am reasoning from the fixed window, per the divergence note — full history puts it at only +0.75 because the period under test has been absorbed into "normal"). The panel role binds: this establishes that something is specific to AI-exposed work, not that work was destroyed. Perfect reallocation would produce exactly this reading. So on its own it does nothing but license the question.

*Inversion.* The strongest opposite reading: this gap's full-history trough was -5.22 in November 2023, so it has *narrowed by 2.7 points* while firm AI adoption climbed from 17.3% to 21.7%. A divergence that peaked before the tools diffused and has been shrinking since looks like the 2021-22 hiring correction decaying, not an AI signal ramping. The gap is also flat over the last four readings — the "2 consecutive readings past the alarm line spanning 1 month" is a level parked past a line, not a fresh widening. And half the gap is the *control* side being strong: if the exposed outflow went into construction, health and leisure, this panel's maximally negative reading is what benign job-switching looks like. Finally the industry proxy is crude — a janitor in the information sector counts as exposed, a data analyst in manufacturing does not.

*Residual after the hiring correction.* The correction explains the shape and much of the magnitude of 2023-24. What it explains less well four years on is exposed employment being *negative in level* in mid-2026 with controls healthy, a curve that is not inverted, and adoption rising. That residual is what I am reading, and it is thin.

**reabsorption (REABSORPTION, as_of 2026-06, 2 months old).** The reading rule binds: the headline 12-month change places the axis; the four secondary readouts are context; the 3-month figures are context at one further remove.

- Headline: 80.2%, -0.5 over 12 months, deviation +1.77 (fixed window; the two baselines agree here, so this does not depend on the window). That is past the panel's registered deterioration threshold of 1 SD. Direction: falling. Level: 0.25 points *above* 2019, which is the panel's own reminder that the level is slow to register a fresh turn from a high start.
- Decomposition: employed -1,436k (-1.38%), population -952k. Per the caveat I discount the population leg hardest and do not quote its size — the January 2026 control revision put a ~-1.5M level shift into it. What the decomposition *does* settle is the direction question: employment is falling, so the ratio is not falling merely because more people arrived. That is the single most load-bearing fact in this reading.
- Long-term unemployed share 27.3%, +4.0 over 12 months, deviation +0.96 (just shy of the attention line). Rising, and 3-month +1.9 agrees. Exits are increasingly not being caught quickly.
- Underemployment gap 3.7, +0.1 over 12 months, deviation +1.48 on the fixed window (past attention). Small in level terms; the 3-month is flat and disagrees with the 12-month, so I treat this as weak.
- Layoffs 1.1, -0.1 over 12 months, deviation -0.34, i.e. *below* norm and falling. Paired with a hires rate of 3.4 against quits 2.0, the panel's own pairing rule says this is a FROZEN market, not a shedding one: incumbents are not being pushed out, the burden is on entrants and on people who have already left. That materially changes the character of the story. If AI is removing work here it is doing it through the hiring channel, not through layoffs, and a frozen market can produce a falling employment share with nobody being fired.
- Hires minus quits 1.4, +0.1 over 12 months, deviation -0.9, i.e. further *away* from displacement. Name the moving side: the net improved because quits fell to 2.0, not because hiring is strong — a 3.4 hires rate is low by 2010s standards. A net figure improving on falling quits is a frozen market again, not absorption.

*Inversion of the reabsorption panel.* The best opposite case is strong. (i) The whole 12-month decline is inside the last quarter: 12m change -0.5 and 3m change -0.5 are the same number, so this is one quarter of evidence, not a year of it, in a survey whose response rates degraded through late 2025 and which lost October 2025 entirely on the companion tracker. (ii) The level is still above 2019. (iii) Layoffs below norm and net hiring up are what a market that is *not* removing people looks like. (iv) Economy-wide, payrolls are +57k and unemployment is 4.2% — I flag explicitly that those are economy-wide CES/CPS headline figures and cannot be used as evidence about exposed industries, but they are legitimate evidence against the claim that the *aggregate* is failing to absorb, which is precisely what this panel is for. Three of the readouts I lean on (headline, long-term share, U6-U3) are the same household survey, so their agreement is weaker than it looks.

I considered whether the population-control revision could be manufacturing the headline fall and therefore the whole verdict. The panel asserts employment is seasonally adjusted and does not carry the same discontinuity, and that the ratio is computed consistently within a control regime. I am not fully persuaded — CPS employment *levels* are reweighted by the same controls, and the -1,436k employment change is suspiciously close in magnitude to the stated ~-1.5M January control shift. I am recording that as the single largest fragility in this reading rather than as a confounder, because the published *ratio* is the measure the panel says to trust and it fell on both horizons.

**exposed_vs_control_wages (ATTRIBUTION, as_of 2026-06).** Exposed pay +4.63% YoY, control +3.53%, differential +1.11, deviation -0.82 (further *away* from displacement), 23 consecutive readings inside its 2010s range. The weighting rule binds and disqualifies this from being strong support for either side, because exposed employment is falling (-1.27%): if entry-level hiring in exposed industries has stopped, the survivors skew senior and the average rises with nobody getting a raise. Note also the one-month jump from +0.71 (May) to +1.11 (June) against a panel described as flat over four readings — that looks like noise and I would not build anything on it. Composition question: unresolved, and it weakens the panel. This is the *only* exposed-specific candidate for positive evidence that exposed workers are being made more valuable, and it cannot carry that weight — which is the main reason I did not read AUGMENTATION.

**individual_wage_growth (COMPOSITION_CONTROL, as_of 2026-06).** Stayers 3.6, switchers 4.4, premium 0.8, deviation -0.54 (away from displacement), recovering over the last four readings. Economy-wide, so it can never attribute anything to exposed work. Its job is the cross-check: it is *not* flat-or-falling while the industry average accelerates, so the crude "the acceleration is pure composition" story is not confirmed either. That leaves the composition question genuinely unresolved rather than resolved in my favour, and I have treated it that way. Substantively, a positive switcher premium is the cleanest single piece of evidence against my verdict: people who move jobs are still landing better than people who stay, which is opportunity-driven mobility, not distress mobility. It is economy-wide, and it is a median, so a collapse concentrated in a minority of exposed workers is exactly the shape it would miss.

**job_postings_spread (ATTRIBUTION, as_of 2026-07, 1 month old — the freshest attribution panel).** Sides named: exposed knowledge-work postings 76.9, i.e. 23.1% *below* their own February 2020 level; control hands-on postings 105.3, i.e. 5.3% *above* theirs. Per the weighting rule I read the change, not the level: spread_change_over_6_months is +2.6, meaning the gap has *narrowed* over six months, and the current -28.4 is narrower than its own 2023-2026 mean of -33.5 (deviation -1.17, away from displacement). No usable pre-2020 baseline, no threshold, and its level is substantially a 2022 rates event still sitting there. So this panel cuts *against* my verdict on the only dimension it is allowed to speak on. It is the leading indicator and it is the freshest attribution reading I have, and I am reading displacement anyway — that is the largest single reason this is LOW and not MEDIUM. Against it: postings easing by 2.6 index points over six months from -28.4 is a modest move on a series whose own history spans -42.8 to -21.4, and it is an advertised intention, not a filled job. The month-over-month move flagged in what_changed (-28.1 to -28.4, same reading date 2026-07, so a revision rather than a new observation) is trivial and I give it no weight.

**labor_productivity (GAINS_TEST, as_of 2026-03, 5 months old).** 2.8% YoY, up from 2.5%, inside the 2.7-3.4 internet-boom band for one quarter, roughly +1.4 SD above the pre-2020 mean of 1.27. Economy-wide, heavily revised, and it cannot attribute anything to AI. Read as the role instructs: gains *are* visible in the aggregate, which is what augmentation working would look like — and it is the strongest thing on this dashboard pointing at augmentation. It does not reach the two-quarters-above-3.4 break. Vintage gap: this is 5 months older than the attribution and reabsorption panels, so the counterweight to my verdict on the gains side cannot yet reflect a recent turn; but note the asymmetry runs the *other* way here too, in that the evidence arguing against me (postings, 2026-07) is in one case *newer* than the evidence supporting me (jobs and reabsorption, 2026-06). I am stating that plainly: my freshest panel disagrees with me.

**worker_share_of_income (DESCRIPTIVE, no vote, as_of 2026-03).** 51.0%, four consecutive quarterly declines, -0.96 over four quarters against a forty-year drift of -0.13/year, in the fastest 10% of declines on record and at the bottom of its full history. I am not counting this, per the panel role, and correctly so: ordinary recessions produced -2.18 and -1.59. But it is worth recording that labour's share is falling at roughly seven times the secular pace in the same quarter that productivity printed 2.8%. Productivity gains that do not reach workers is the shape a displacement story would have, and this panel is barred from voting on it. Economy-wide either way.

**ai_adoption (DEPLOYMENT_GATE, as_of 2026-07).** 21.7% of firms, monotone-ish from 17.3% in November 2025, and a size gradient of 1.87 (38.8% at 250+ employees vs 20.8% at 1-4), so worker exposure exceeds the firm share. The gate is open: a displacement reading is permitted. It causes nothing. I list it as load-bearing only in the sense that without it the word "AI" could not attach to the reading at all. *Inversion:* adoption of a tool in "any business function" is a very low bar — it includes a marketing team using a chatbot — and rising adoption alongside a *narrowing* exposed-vs-control gap since 2023 is arguably evidence against the causal link.

**Panels that contribute nothing, read anyway.** ai_use_automation_vs_augmentation is 11 months stale and essentially unchanged across three releases (43.1/56.9); I note only that the split has been stable, and it measures one vendor's conversations, not jobs. ai_capability_metr (as_of 2026-04) shows an 80% horizon of 186 minutes for the leading model, a large jump over the field; ai_capability_gdpval_ratings has Anthropic leading OpenAI by ~125 Elo; ai_capability_vs_human_experts shows 70.9% wins-plus-ties but 49.7% wins-only, i.e. just under true parity, self-reported, and nothing published since December 2025. Interesting, and counted in nothing: a model clearing an expert on a benchmark is not an employer deciding to stop paying that expert, and none of these can corroborate a labor reading in either direction. I have not used them.

**Macro / cyclical test.** macro_regime (as_of 2026-08): curve +0.5 and not inverted, real 10-year 2.5%, expected inflation 2.3%. Per the role, this can name the cyclical hypothesis and can never clear it, and I have not used it to exculpate anything. The contemporaneous test is the one that matters, and I ran it on the controls: control industry jobs +1.27% YoY, control pay +3.53%, control postings 5.3% *above* their own February 2020 level, layoffs economy-wide at 1.1 and falling. A general macro contraction would have pulled the control side down with the exposed side, and it has not. That cuts in my favour. Where it cuts against me: the *aggregate* reabsorption weakness I am leaning on is economy-wide, and if the exposed side alone is weak then a falling economy-wide prime-age employment share needs a source outside exposed industries — which is either an artefact (see the population-control worry) or a genuine broad softening that the controls are not showing. That tension is unresolved and it is a real hole in my reading, not a rhetorical concession.

**Why not CONFOUNDED.** I can name candidate causes — the 2021-22 hiring correction, the 2022 rate shock still sitting in the postings level, and the January 2026 Census population-control revision. The first two are weighed against my reading, not alongside it, and neither is a live 2026 event: the correction's peak effect was the -5.22 gap in late 2023 and the postings spread has been flat since 2022, so both are decaying, not driving. The third is the closest to a genuine confounder and it has a series behind it (decomposition.population_change_thousands -952, with a stated ~-1.5M control shift), but the panel states the published ratio is computed consistently within a control regime and it is the ratio that fell on both horizons. Mixed evidence is not grounds for CONFOUNDED, so I take the directional reading and put the weakness in the rating.

**News.** BLS Employment Situation through 2026-06: payrolls 158,984k, +57k on the month, unemployment 4.2%. That is economy-wide establishment data and I do not pair it with exposed-industry figures; it is legitimate counterweight to the household survey's absorption failure, and I have counted it as such. +57k is soft but positive, and 4.2% is not a market removing work at scale. The AP items reference an Iran war, inflation, the Fed and mortgages. An energy or conflict shock could move hiring, but it would show up in controls too — construction and leisure are more rate- and energy-sensitive than information services — and both are strong; it is also too recent to sit inside June data, and it does not explain why exposed-industry *pay* is running 1.1 points ahead of control. The mortgage/Fed thread is the one worth flagging: rate-sensitive white-collar hiring is exactly the 2022 mechanism the postings panel attributes its level to, so if rates are again the story, the postings spread should be *widening* — it is narrowing (+2.6 over six months), so I set that hypothesis aside. The "job openings" item is JOLTS commentary and the JOLTS series themselves are in the panel (hires 3.4, quits 2.0, layoffs 1.1); the series, not the coverage, is what I read. No news item in this package attributes headcount decisions to AI, so I have no employer-incentive-contaminated claim to discount this run. News generated hypotheses and moved nothing.

**Overturn design.** My verdict is displacement, so the overturn condition must be the labour market absorbing people again. Primary: reabsorption headline.change_over_12_months at_or_above 0.0. Current -0.5; pre-2020 SD of 12-month changes is 0.52 and the pre-2020 mean is +0.42, so 0.0 is well inside one SD of normal and the series demonstrably traversed 0.5 points in the last single quarter, which is why I judge it reachable inside 90 days. It is monthly and publishes three more times before 2026-11-02, so the window cannot close without observations — unlike the quarterly productivity and income-share panels, where a 90-day test could see literally nothing new. Discrimination check: what else carries this to ≥0.0? An ordinary rebound would, but an ordinary rebound *is* my reading being wrong, since my reading is built on this series falling. A January population-control revision cannot land before November. A seasonal artefact cannot, because this is a 12-month change on a seasonally adjusted series. Secondary, to stop a single noisy print from overturning and to require that people are actually landing: secondary.long_term_unemployed_share.latest_value at_or_below 25.0, against 27.3 now and a 12-month rise of 4.0 with a 12-month SD of 5.2, so a 2.3-point retracement is well inside this series' demonstrated volatility. Both must hold. I considered using hires_minus_quits or layoffs_rate as the second condition and rejected both: they already read *away* from displacement (-0.9 and -0.34 deviation), so a threshold there would be tripped by the status quo and would discriminate nothing — the same error as setting a trigger at a level a known confounder already reached. I also considered requiring the exposed-vs-control differential to heal above -2.2, but that measures reallocation, not absorption, and my verdict turns on absorption; a healed gap with absorption still failing would not make me wrong in the way that matters.

**What would make me wrong in a way this test would not catch:** if the household survey's prime-age fall turns out to be a weighting artefact that is silently revised rather than reversed in the published 12-month change. I cannot construct a mechanical guard against that from these panels, and I am recording it here so a later run can hold me to it.

pass2.notificationLine: Nothing new this month; displacement holds on prime-age employment down 0.5 points
pass2.publishedNote:
The reading is displacement, held with low confidence, and it rests on deterioration that has actually shown up in the data rather than on an absence of good news.

Nothing moved this month. One of thirteen panels changed, and the change was a small downward revision to a job-postings figure already published for July, not a new observation. Everything below is last month's evidence read again.

What supports the displacement reading: employment in the industries most exposed to AI is shrinking, down 1.27% over the year, while industries AI has barely touched are adding jobs at 1.27%. Meanwhile the share of 25-to-54-year-olds with a job is 80.2%, down half a point over twelve months, and that fall comes from employment dropping by about 1.4 million rather than from a bigger population. A specific slice of the economy losing work while the wider market fails to absorb the outflow is what separates displacement from ordinary reshuffling. The mechanism is a hiring freeze, not firing: layoffs are low at 1.1 and falling, hiring is weak at 3.4, and 27.3% of the unemployed have now been out of work more than six months, up four points in a year. The cost is landing on people trying to get in and people already out.

What argues against it, and this is where the low confidence comes from: the freshest evidence on the dashboard disagrees. Job postings lead everything else here, and the shortfall in postings for exposed knowledge work — currently about 23% below its February 2020 level, against hands-on work sitting about 5% above its own — has been closing over the past six months, not widening. Much of that level is a hangover from the 2022 interest-rate shock. On a longer view the exposed-industry job shortfall was worse in late 2023, before AI tools diffused widely, and has narrowed while firm adoption climbed from 17.3% to 21.7% since November. A signal loudest before the tools arrived looks more like the 2021-22 over-hiring correction unwinding. Pay also runs the wrong way for displacement: exposed industries are paying 4.63% growth against 3.53% in control industries, though that could simply be entry-level hiring stopping and the remaining workforce skewing senior. Economy-wide, job switchers still earn 4.4% growth against 3.6% for stayers, which is opportunity-driven mobility, not distress — that figure covers the whole workforce, not exposed industries, so distress concentrated among a minority is exactly what it would miss. Productivity at 2.8% a year, against a pre-2020 norm near 1.3%, is the strongest sign pointing at augmentation, and it too is economy-wide.

One thing readers relying on the prime-age employment figure are owed: it may not be trustworthy. The entire twelve-month fall happened inside the most recent quarter, and the January population-control revision pushed a level shift of roughly 1.5 million into this survey — close to the 1.4 million employment drop doing the work here. The published ratio is meant to be consistent within a control regime and fell on both the quarterly and annual views, which is why I have not called this a confounder. But if that fall is revised away rather than reversed, the displacement reading loses its load-bearing fact. Separately, payrolls rose 57,000 in June and unemployment is 4.2%, both economy-wide, and neither looks like a market removing work at scale.

Watch the prime-age employment share chart. If it climbs back to flat or better against a year earlier, the market is catching exits again and this reading was wrong.
pass2.fullAnalysis:
The reading is displacement, and it is held with low confidence.

It matters what that rests on. This is not a case of saying displacement has not started and there is nothing to see; the reading rests on deterioration that has actually been observed in the data, not on the absence of good news. Two things are happening at once. Job growth in the industries most exposed to AI is negative: employment in those industries is down 1.27% over the past year, while the comparison industries AI has barely touched are adding jobs at 1.27%. And the wider labour market is not visibly catching the people leaving: the share of Americans aged 25 to 54 with a job is 80.2%, down half a point over twelve months, and the drop comes from employment falling by about 1.4 million rather than from population growth. When a specific slice of the economy is shedding work and the aggregate is not soaking it up, that is the combination that separates displacement from ordinary reshuffling.

Nothing moved this month. Of the thirteen panels, one changed, and the change was a small downward revision to a job-postings figure already published for July, not a new observation. The industry job counts, the household employment survey, the pay series, productivity, adoption and the capability benchmarks are all exactly where they were. So this month adds no evidence in either direction, and everything below is the same body of evidence read again.

The character of the exposed-industry weakness is worth spelling out, because it is not mass firing. The layoff rate is 1.1 and falling, below its own normal range. Hiring is weak at 3.4, and quits are down to 2.0. That is a frozen market, not a shedding one: incumbents are not being pushed out, and the cost is falling on people trying to get in and on people who have already left. A market like that can produce a falling employment share with almost nobody being fired. If AI is removing work here, it is doing it through the hiring door rather than the exit door, and that shape also explains why the long-term unemployed share has climbed to 27.3% of the jobless, up four points in a year: exits are increasingly not being caught quickly.

Now the case against, which is strong enough that it holds the confidence down to low.

The freshest evidence on the dashboard disagrees with the displacement reading. Job postings are the leading indicator here, and they are improving. Postings for exposed knowledge work sit about 23% below their February 2020 level while postings for hands-on control work sit about 5% above theirs, which looks damning until you read the direction rather than the level: the shortfall in knowledge-work postings has been closing over the past six months, not widening, and the current gap is narrower than its own average since 2023. Much of that level is a hangover from the 2022 rate shock rather than anything to do with AI. Postings data is one month newer than the industry job counts I am leaning on. So the newest thing I have argues against the verdict I have written, and I am saying so rather than burying it.

The same is true across a longer horizon. The gap between exposed and control industry job growth was far worse in late 2023 than it is now — the exposed side was contracting relative to controls by more than five points then, against two and a half now. That divergence peaked before AI tools diffused widely and has been shrinking while firm adoption rose from 17.3% of businesses last November to 21.7% now. A signal that was loudest before the tools arrived looks more like the 2021-22 over-hiring correction decaying than like an AI effect ramping up. It is also worth noting that half of the current gap is the control side being genuinely strong: if the people leaving exposed industries walked into construction, health care and hospitality, this is what benign job-switching would look like on this chart.

Pay does not behave the way displacement usually does either. Pay in AI-exposed industries is growing at 4.63% a year against 3.53% in the control industries. If AI were making these workers redundant, you would expect their pay to lag, not lead. But this cannot be taken as evidence that exposed workers are being made more valuable, because exposed employment is shrinking at the same time: if entry-level hiring in those industries has stopped, the people left behind skew senior and the average wage rises without anyone getting a raise. I cannot separate those two stories with what is here, which is the main reason I did not read this as augmentation. The one cross-check available is economy-wide, not exposed-specific: people who switch jobs are still getting 4.4% pay growth against 3.6% for those who stay. That premium is not collapsing, which is the single cleanest piece of evidence against the displacement reading — people are still moving jobs for opportunity rather than out of distress. It is a median across the whole workforce, so distress concentrated in a minority of exposed workers is exactly what it would miss.

Productivity is running at 2.8% a year, up from 2.5%, against a pre-2020 norm closer to 1.3%. Gains are visible in the aggregate, which is what augmentation working would look like, and this is the strongest thing here pointing that way. Two caveats: the figure is five months older than the labour panels, and it is economy-wide, so it cannot be attributed to AI or to exposed industries. Alongside it, labour's share of national income has fallen for four straight quarters to 51.0%, about a point over the year against a long-run drift of roughly a tenth of a point a year. Productivity gains that do not reach workers is the shape a displacement story has, though ordinary recessions have produced sharper falls in labour's share than this one.

The largest weakness in this reading is not any of the above; it is a data problem, and readers relying on the prime-age employment figure are owed it. All of the twelve-month fall in the prime-age employment share happened inside the most recent quarter — the twelve-month and three-month changes are the same half point. So this is one quarter of evidence, not a year of it. Worse, the January 2026 Census population-control revision put a level shift of roughly 1.5 million into this survey, and the fall in employment I am leaning on is about 1.4 million, uncomfortably close to that. The published ratio is meant to be computed consistently within a control regime, and it fell on both the twelve-month and three-month views, which is why I have treated the revision as a fragility rather than as an outright alternative explanation. But I am not fully persuaded, and if this fall is quietly revised away rather than reversed, the displacement reading loses its load-bearing fact. The household survey's response rates also degraded through late 2025. Three of the readouts I lean on come from that same survey, so their agreement with each other is worth less than it looks.

Two further tensions I have not resolved. First, the establishment survey disagrees with the household survey at the aggregate level: payrolls rose 57,000 in June and unemployment is 4.2%. Those are economy-wide figures and cannot be used to say anything about exposed industries specifically, but they are legitimate evidence against the claim that the aggregate market is failing to absorb people, which is precisely the claim doing the work here. Second, if weakness is confined to exposed industries while control industries are healthy, then a falling economy-wide employment share needs a source outside exposed industries — which is either a measurement artefact or a broad softening the control industries are not showing. That does not add up cleanly, and I would rather say so than paper over it.

On the cyclical alternative: the yield curve is not inverted, and more to the point, a general downturn would drag the control industries down with the exposed ones. It has not. Control industry jobs, pay and postings are all healthy and layoffs are low, so a plain macro contraction does not fit. The rate-sensitivity story is the one worth watching — white-collar hiring is where the 2022 rate shock landed — but if rates were again the driver, the knowledge-work postings shortfall should be widening, and it is narrowing.

Finally, several panels that get talked about a lot contribute nothing here and I have not used them. AI systems now beat or tie human experts on about 71% of tested work tasks, and win outright just under half the time; the leading model can sustain tasks of roughly three hours at the measured reliability level. A model clearing an expert on a benchmark is not an employer deciding to stop paying that expert. NOTIFICATION: Nothing new this month; displacement holds on prime-age employment down 0.5 points
TAGLINE: Nothing moved, freshest panel disagrees
FULL_ANALYSIS:
The reading is displacement, and it is held with low confidence.

It matters what that rests on. This is not a case of saying displacement has not started and there is nothing to see; the reading rests on deterioration that has actually been observed in the data, not on the absence of good news. Two things are happening at once. Job growth in the industries most exposed to AI is negative: employment in those industries is down 1.27% over the past year, while the comparison industries AI has barely touched are adding jobs at 1.27%. And the wider labour market is not visibly catching the people leaving: the share of Americans aged 25 to 54 with a job is 80.2%, down half a point over twelve months, and the drop comes from employment falling by about 1.4 million rather than from population growth. When a specific slice of the economy is shedding work and the aggregate is not soaking it up, that is the combination that separates displacement from ordinary reshuffling.

Nothing moved this month. Of the thirteen panels, one changed, and the change was a small downward revision to a job-postings figure already published for July, not a new observation. The industry job counts, the household employment survey, the pay series, productivity, adoption and the capability benchmarks are all exactly where they were. So this month adds no evidence in either direction, and everything below is the same body of evidence read again.

The character of the exposed-industry weakness is worth spelling out, because it is not mass firing. The layoff rate is 1.1 and falling, below its own normal range. Hiring is weak at 3.4, and quits are down to 2.0. That is a frozen market, not a shedding one: incumbents are not being pushed out, and the cost is falling on people trying to get in and on people who have already left. A market like that can produce a falling employment share with almost nobody being fired. If AI is removing work here, it is doing it through the hiring door rather than the exit door, and that shape also explains why the long-term unemployed share has climbed to 27.3% of the jobless, up four points in a year: exits are increasingly not being caught quickly.

Now the case against, which is strong enough that it holds the confidence down to low.

The freshest evidence on the dashboard disagrees with the displacement reading. Job postings are the leading indicator here, and they are improving. Postings for exposed knowledge work sit about 23% below their February 2020 level while postings for hands-on control work sit about 5% above theirs, which looks damning until you read the direction rather than the level: the shortfall in knowledge-work postings has been closing over the past six months, not widening, and the current gap is narrower than its own average since 2023. Much of that level is a hangover from the 2022 rate shock rather than anything to do with AI. Postings data is one month newer than the industry job counts I am leaning on. So the newest thing I have argues against the verdict I have written, and I am saying so rather than burying it.

The same is true across a longer horizon. The gap between exposed and control industry job growth was far worse in late 2023 than it is now — the exposed side was contracting relative to controls by more than five points then, against two and a half now. That divergence peaked before AI tools diffused widely and has been shrinking while firm adoption rose from 17.3% of businesses last November to 21.7% now. A signal that was loudest before the tools arrived looks more like the 2021-22 over-hiring correction decaying than like an AI effect ramping up. It is also worth noting that half of the current gap is the control side being genuinely strong: if the people leaving exposed industries walked into construction, health care and hospitality, this is what benign job-switching would look like on this chart.

Pay does not behave the way displacement usually does either. Pay in AI-exposed industries is growing at 4.63% a year against 3.53% in the control industries. If AI were making these workers redundant, you would expect their pay to lag, not lead. But this cannot be taken as evidence that exposed workers are being made more valuable, because exposed employment is shrinking at the same time: if entry-level hiring in those industries has stopped, the people left behind skew senior and the average wage rises without anyone getting a raise. I cannot separate those two stories with what is here, which is the main reason I did not read this as augmentation. The one cross-check available is economy-wide, not exposed-specific: people who switch jobs are still getting 4.4% pay growth against 3.6% for those who stay. That premium is not collapsing, which is the single cleanest piece of evidence against the displacement reading — people are still moving jobs for opportunity rather than out of distress. It is a median across the whole workforce, so distress concentrated in a minority of exposed workers is exactly what it would miss.

Productivity is running at 2.8% a year, up from 2.5%, against a pre-2020 norm closer to 1.3%. Gains are visible in the aggregate, which is what augmentation working would look like, and this is the strongest thing here pointing that way. Two caveats: the figure is five months older than the labour panels, and it is economy-wide, so it cannot be attributed to AI or to exposed industries. Alongside it, labour's share of national income has fallen for four straight quarters to 51.0%, about a point over the year against a long-run drift of roughly a tenth of a point a year. Productivity gains that do not reach workers is the shape a displacement story has, though ordinary recessions have produced sharper falls in labour's share than this one.

The largest weakness in this reading is not any of the above; it is a data problem, and readers relying on the prime-age employment figure are owed it. All of the twelve-month fall in the prime-age employment share happened inside the most recent quarter — the twelve-month and three-month changes are the same half point. So this is one quarter of evidence, not a year of it. Worse, the January 2026 Census population-control revision put a level shift of roughly 1.5 million into this survey, and the fall in employment I am leaning on is about 1.4 million, uncomfortably close to that. The published ratio is meant to be computed consistently within a control regime, and it fell on both the twelve-month and three-month views, which is why I have treated the revision as a fragility rather than as an outright alternative explanation. But I am not fully persuaded, and if this fall is quietly revised away rather than reversed, the displacement reading loses its load-bearing fact. The household survey's response rates also degraded through late 2025. Three of the readouts I lean on come from that same survey, so their agreement with each other is worth less than it looks.

Two further tensions I have not resolved. First, the establishment survey disagrees with the household survey at the aggregate level: payrolls rose 57,000 in June and unemployment is 4.2%. Those are economy-wide figures and cannot be used to say anything about exposed industries specifically, but they are legitimate evidence against the claim that the aggregate market is failing to absorb people, which is precisely the claim doing the work here. Second, if weakness is confined to exposed industries while control industries are healthy, then a falling economy-wide employment share needs a source outside exposed industries — which is either a measurement artefact or a broad softening the control industries are not showing. That does not add up cleanly, and I would rather say so than paper over it.

On the cyclical alternative: the yield curve is not inverted, and more to the point, a general downturn would drag the control industries down with the exposed ones. It has not. Control industry jobs, pay and postings are all healthy and layoffs are low, so a plain macro contraction does not fit. The rate-sensitivity story is the one worth watching — white-collar hiring is where the 2022 rate shock landed — but if rates were again the driver, the knowledge-work postings shortfall should be widening, and it is narrowing.

Finally, several panels that get talked about a lot contribute nothing here and I have not used them. AI systems now beat or tie human experts on about 71% of tested work tasks, and win outright just under half the time; the leading model can sustain tasks of roughly three hours at the measured reliability level. A model clearing an expert on a benchmark is not an employer deciding to stop paying that expert. Adoption at 21.7% of firms — with 38.8% of large employers using AI in some function against 20.8% of the smallest — establishes only that the tools are in the building in sufficient numbers for a displacement story to be possible at all. It causes nothing by itself, and the bar for counting as an adopter is low.

What would move first if this is turning: the prime-age employment share. If it climbs back to flat or better against a year earlier while the long-term unemployed share retreats, the aggregate market is catching exits again and the displacement reading was wrong. That series publishes monthly, so there will be three more observations before the end of October.

pass1.confidenceBasis: Corroborating — exposed_vs_control_jobs (exposed -1.27% YoY vs control +1.27%, differential -2.54, 2.08 SD past the clean pre-2020 baseline and past its -2.48 trigger; as_of 2026-06) and reabsorption (headline prime-age EPOP 12m change -0.5, 1.77 SD worse than the pre-2020 norm and past its own 1-SD deterioration rule, with prime-age employment itself down 1,436k, long-term-unemployed share +4.0pp to 27.3%, U6-U3 gap 1.48 SD; as_of 2026-06); failing to corroborate or cutting against — job_postings_spread (spread has NARROWED 2.6 over six months, and it is the leading and better-exposure-proxied panel, as_of 2026-07), labor_productivity (2.8%, 1.37 SD above the pre-2020 mean, inside the internet-boom band, as_of 2026-03 and therefore an older counterweight than the panels supporting me), JOLTS layoffs 1.1 and falling and hires-minus-quits 1.4 both sitting on the away-from-displacement side, individual_wage_growth switcher premium +0.8 saying movers are still landing well economy-wide, exposed_vs_control_wages +1.11 (unusable as support either way under its own weighting rule since exposed employment is falling); UNMET DOUBTS — two of the three: the headline absorption move is one quarter of evidence, not a year (3-month change -0.5 equals the 12-month change -0.5), and the leading indicator (postings) is pointing the other way.

falsifier.unit: percentage points of the 25-54 population, change over 12 months

pass1.falsifierPlain: If the prime-age employment-rate chart stops falling year-over-year (12-month change back to -0.1 or better) while the exposed-minus-control jobs gap also pulls back inside its -2.48 trigger to -2.2 or narrower, then the outflow was being absorbed and this displacement reading was wrong.
pass1.reasoningLog:
**Headline framing.** This is a DISPLACEMENT reading and it rests on positive evidence of deterioration, not on absence of improvement: prime-age employment is down 1,436k over twelve months on the household survey, the prime-age employment share's 12-month change is -0.5 (1.77 SD worse than its clean 2010-2019 norm and past the panel's own registered deterioration rule of 1 SD), and the long-term-unemployed share is up 4.0 points to 27.3%. That is absorption failing, not merely absorption not improving. It is LOW confidence because the absorption deterioration is one quarter old, the attribution gap has stopped widening, and the earliest-moving panel is pointing the other way.

**Panel by panel.**

*exposed_vs_control_jobs (ATTRIBUTION, as_of 2026-06, 2 months old).* Exposed industries -1.27% YoY; control +1.27% YoY. Name both sides: exposed is contracting outright, control is growing at a healthy clip. Differential -2.54, past the -2.48 trigger, 2.08 SD past the fixed pre-2020 baseline (I use the pre-2020 figure per the divergence note; against full history it reads only 0.75 SD, which is what contamination looks like). This is the contemporaneous macro test and it passes: if the weakness were a general cycle, construction/leisure/education-health would be weak too, and they are adding jobs. The yield curve (+0.4, not inverted) cannot exculpate weakness already in the data and I am not using it that way; I note only that the bond market is not independently pricing a recession. Industry-proxy caveat noted: a janitor in the information sector counts as exposed, so I attribute no precision to this split.

But the panel's own weighting rule binds and I apply it: a widening gap is EXACTLY what perfect reallocation would produce. Control industries growing at +1.27% is arithmetically consistent with them absorbing everyone who left exposed work. This panel alone establishes only that something is specific to AI-exposed work. Also: the gap is not widening. Prior -2.61, now -2.54, "holding roughly flat over the last 4 readings." A parked gap is a standing condition, and the trigger fires on level, which means it can sit tripped without telling me anything new this month.

*The 2021-22 hiring correction.* Information and professional/business services over-hired in 2021-22 and have been unwinding since; this predates current tools and I weigh it against, not alongside. It explains: a large share of the exposed employment decline, the fact that the postings spread opened in 2022 (the panel's own artifact attributes the opening substantially to the rate cycle, not model releases), and much of the level of the current gap. What it leaves as residual: it is now roughly four years old and a correction should be decaying, yet exposed employment is still contracting in absolute terms in mid-2026 while control grows; and a hiring correction in two sectors does not obviously explain a 1.4-million fall in prime-age employment economy-wide or a 4-point rise in the long-term-unemployed share. That residual is what I am reading as displacement, and it is thin.

*reabsorption (REABSORPTION, as_of 2026-06).* The panel binds: the headline decides, the four secondaries are context, the 3-month horizons are context at one further remove. Headline: 80.2, 12-month change -0.5, falling, 1.77 SD past the pre-2020 norm; the two baselines agree here so the reading does not depend on the window. Decomposition direction check: employed_change -1,436k, i.e. employment itself is down, so the ratio is not falling merely because the denominator grew. I deliberately do not quote the population leg (Census control revisions put a -1.5M level shift into January 2026) and I do not net this against the +57k CES payroll print in the news package — different survey, different ages, different horizon, and the panel explicitly forbids that comparison. Level: still 0.25 points ABOVE 2019, which is a genuine mitigant and I state it. The fast horizon (-0.5 over three months, 2.85 SD) agrees in direction, but that agreement is also the problem: the whole twelve-month move sits inside the last quarter. That is one quarter of evidence dressed as a year.

Secondaries, read as context: long-term-unemployed share 27.3%, +4.0 over 12 months — large in level terms but only 0.96 SD against its own very noisy history (SD of 12m changes is 5.2), so it is suggestive rather than decisive; +1.9 over three months, same direction. U6-U3 at 3.7, +0.1, 1.48 SD against the fixed window — mildly deteriorating, small in absolute terms, and the 3-month change is flat, so the two horizons disagree and I am citing the 12-month one. Hires-minus-quits 1.4, +0.1 over 12 months, reading 0.9 SD AWAY from displacement — but name the moving side: hires 3.4, quits 2.0. The net is comfortable because quitting is depressed, not because hiring is strong. Layoffs 1.1 and falling, 0.34 SD away from displacement. Applying the panel's own pairing rule: weak hiring plus layoffs at-or-below norm is a FROZEN market, not a shedding one. Incumbents are not being pushed out; the burden is falling on entrants and on people already outside. That is compatible with AI-driven displacement operating through non-replacement rather than firing — which is what I think is most likely if this reading is right — but it is equally compatible with an ordinary late-cycle hiring freeze. I record that honestly.

*job_postings_spread (ATTRIBUTION, as_of 2026-07, the freshest labor panel).* Both sides named: knowledge-work postings 76.9, i.e. 23.1% below their own Feb-2020 level; hands-on postings 105.3, 5.3% above theirs. The panel's weighting rule says read the change, not the level, because the level is substantially a 2022 rate event. The change over six months is +2.6 — the spread has NARROWED. Against the contaminated 2023-26 history the current reading is 1.17 SD less extreme than average. This cuts against my verdict, and it cuts hard for two reasons: postings lead headcount, and this panel is cut by occupation rather than industry, which the payload itself says is the better exposure proxy. So the panel most likely to be right first, on the better proxy, says exposed demand is stabilising or slightly improving. I am not treating hands-on strength as absorption — the panel is explicit that demand rotating between kinds of work is not workers rotating with it, and a posting is an advertised intention. But the narrowing on the exposed side is a genuine counter-signal and it is the main reason I am at LOW rather than MEDIUM. Note the vintage: this panel (2026-07) is one month fresher than the panels supporting me (2026-06), so the counter-signal is not stale — it is the supporting evidence that is slightly older.

*exposed_vs_control_wages (ATTRIBUTION, as_of 2026-06).* Exposed pay +4.63%, control +3.53%, differential +1.11, up from 0.71 last month, and 0.82 SD AWAY from displacement. I am not citing this as support for either side, because the panel's weighting rule binds: exposed employment is falling (-1.27%), so the composition artifact is live and this average cannot distinguish augmentation from displacement. Mechanically, if entry-level hiring in information and professional services has stopped, the remaining workforce skews senior and the average rises with nobody getting a raise. The cross-check confirms the worry rather than dispelling it: individual_wage_growth (same people, twelve months apart) has stayers at 3.6 and switchers at 4.4, neither accelerating, while the industry average jumped 0.4 points in a single month. The composition question is therefore unresolved and I let it weaken the panel rather than reporting +1.11 at face value. This is also the single cleanest instance in the payload of the population-under-the-average changing.

*individual_wage_growth (COMPOSITION_CONTROL, as_of 2026-06).* Switcher premium +0.8, 0.54 SD away from displacement, recovering over the last four readings. Read as designed: it disqualifies the industry pay panel as evidence, and it says that economy-wide, people who move jobs are being bid for. That is the strongest single piece of evidence against my verdict on the "did they land well" question, and I flag that it is ECONOMY-WIDE and therefore cannot speak to exposed workers specifically. Two things blunt it: it is a median, so a collapse concentrated in a minority is exactly the shape it misses, and the CPS underneath it is degraded (October 2025 missing entirely). It does not overturn the reading; it does keep me from rating it MEDIUM.

*labor_productivity (GAINS_TEST, as_of 2026-03, 5 months old).* 2.8%, up from 2.5%, inside the 2.7-3.4 internet-boom band for one quarter, 1.37 SD above the pre-2020 mean. Per the panel role, gains showing up is what augmentation working would look like, and this is the most substantive augmentation-side evidence on the board. Two qualifications I hold against it: it is economy-wide and can never attribute anything to AI-exposed work, and output-per-hour rises arithmetically when hours fall faster than output — which is also what a displacement episode produces. The break rule requires two straight quarters above 3.4 and we have one quarter at 2.8, so nothing has broken. Vintage: 2026-03 versus 2026-06 for the jobs and reabsorption panels — a one-quarter gap, at the edge of what can be compared without comment, so I comment: the panel arguing against me is older than the panels arguing for me and cannot yet reflect a turn in either direction.

*worker_share_of_income (DESCRIPTIVE, no vote, as_of 2026-03).* 51.0%, four consecutive quarterly declines, -1.0 over four quarters, in the fastest decile of declines on record, and below the previous full-history low of 51.19. Economy-wide and falling for forty years for pre-AI reasons; the panel explicitly says any trigger here fires on recessions. Noted as evocative — productivity elevated while labor's share falls at an unusual pace is the shape of gains not reaching workers — and counted as zero, per its panel_role.

*ai_adoption (DEPLOYMENT_GATE, as_of 2026-07).* 21.5% of firms, up from 17.3% in November 2025, and the size gradient (36.8% at 250+ employees against 20.8% at 1-4) means worker exposure exceeds the firm share. I do not state a worker-weighted number because the payload says none is measured. The gate is open, which PERMITS a displacement reading and causes nothing. Note the reading moved 21.7 → 21.5 for the same July date since the last run — a revision or panel-rotation effect, exactly the noise the artifact warns about, and it does not change the direction over nine collections.

*Panels counted in nothing.* ai_capability_metr, ai_capability_gdpval_ratings, ai_capability_vs_human_experts, ai_use_automation_vs_augmentation. Read them; none corroborate a labor reading in either direction. Worth noting for the record only: GDPval-AA top Elo moved 1860.6 → 1845.4 across a pool re-read, and the human-baseline panel has published nothing since 2025-12 (8 months stale, self-reported by the vendor whose model leads, and 70.9% is wins-plus-ties against a true-parity figure of 49.7%). The automation/augmentation split is 11 months old and has been flat across three releases; it predates every labor month here and I give it no weight.

**Inversions of my own supporting panels.**

exposed_vs_control_jobs, best opposite case: this is the maximally-negative-under-perfect-reallocation panel, and the control side is growing at exactly the rate needed to absorb the exposed outflow. Add the 2021-22 correction, which predates AI and is a sufficient cause for a multi-year unwind in these two sectors, and the gap has stopped widening (-2.61 → -2.54, flat over four readings). Read that way, this panel shows a stabilising post-boom normalisation with workers rotating into hands-on work, which is benign job-switching and not displacement. I cannot refute this from within the panel; it is why the panel cannot carry the verdict alone.

reabsorption, best opposite case: the level is still above 2019, layoffs are low and falling, and hires-minus-quits sits on the healthy side. The entire 12-month deterioration in the headline occurred in the last three months, on a household survey with documented response-rate degradation through this period, in a year that also carried a -1.5M January population-control revision. A single noisy quarter in the CPS is a completely ordinary thing to see, and the honest opposite reading is: nothing has happened to absorption, and I am reading survey noise. This is the doubt I am least able to answer, and it is the reason for LOW.

ai_adoption, best opposite case: it counts firms one-vote-each over a rotating respondent panel, so the rise could be who answered rather than who adopted, and even at face value adoption is not an event in anyone's employment. Also, augmentation requires adoption just as much as displacement does — a rising gate is equally consistent with firms deploying tools that make existing staff more productive, which is what the productivity panel might be showing. No reading of this panel is displacement-specific.

**Hypotheses I rejected.**

CONFOUNDED via the 2022 rate shock / rate-sensitive white-collar hiring: named cause, and the job_postings_spread measurement_artifact is the series that supports it. I rejected it as a verdict because it explains the LEVEL of the postings spread (a 2022 event still sitting there) and a good part of the exposed jobs decline, but it does not explain why prime-age employment is falling now, in mid-2026, while control industries add jobs and the curve is un-inverted at +0.4. The payload's instruction is to weigh the hiring correction against displacement and report the residual, not to convert it into a non-answer, and "mixed evidence" is explicitly not grounds for CONFOUNDED.

CONFOUNDED via general recession: fails the contemporaneous test. Control industries are at +1.27% YoY and control postings are 5.3% above their own pre-pandemic level. A general slump pulls both sides down together, and it has not.

AUGMENTATION: the affirmative case would be productivity at 2.8% plus exposed pay growth ahead of control. The second leg is disqualified by the panel's own weighting rule (exposed employment falling → composition artifact live → cannot be cited as strong support for either side), and confirmed as suspect by the composition control, which shows no acceleration for the same people. That leaves an economy-wide productivity number, which by its panel_role cannot attribute anything to exposed work, is 5 months old, and has one quarter inside its band against a two-quarter break rule. Augmentation working needs positive evidence that exposed workers are being made more valuable; I do not have a composition-immune, exposed-industry version of that anywhere on this dashboard. So augmentation would have had to rest largely on the absence of catastrophe, and there is deterioration present, so it cannot even rest there.

**News, considered and mostly set aside.**

Iran war (three AP items reference it). Plausible mechanism: energy prices, uncertainty, hiring freezes. Set aside for this reading because it is too recent to be in June data, and more importantly it would hit construction and leisure/hospitality at least as hard as information and professional services — control is at +1.27%, so a war-driven demand shock is not what is producing an exposed-specific gap.

Fed / mortgage / inflation coverage. This is the live version of the rate confounder and it matters most for the postings panel, whose spread the payload already attributes substantially to the 2022 tightening. Relevant, already discounted in how I read that panel, and it argues for reading the postings LEVEL as history rather than news — which is what I did.

BLS Employment Situation, payrolls 158,984k, +57k, U3 4.2% (through 2026-06). Economy-wide, so it may not be used as evidence about exposed industries. It is weak-but-positive establishment-survey growth sitting beside a sharply negative CPS prime-age twelve-month figure; per the reabsorption panel's explicit caveat these are three differences at once (survey, age range, horizon) and neither refutes the other. I did not net them. What +57k does do is make the "control industries are booming and absorbing everyone" story less comfortable than the +1.27% control figure alone suggests: aggregate hiring is barely positive.

pass2.publishedNote:
The reading is still displacement, held with low confidence, and it rests on positive evidence of deterioration rather than on the absence of good news: employment among 25-to-54-year-olds is down about 1.44 million over twelve months, and the share of unemployed people who have been out of work more than six months has risen 4.0 points to 27.3%.

Nothing in the labor data moved this month. Jobs, the employment rate, pay, postings and productivity all carry the same readings as last month. Three numbers changed and none of them concerns workers: the share of firms using AI was restated at 21.5% for July rather than 21.7% for the same month, a survey revision rather than adoption falling; a macro summary ticked down a tenth; one AI capability score fell on a re-scored pool.

The clearest support is that the weakness is specific to AI-exposed work. Information and professional services are shrinking outright, down 1.27% over the year, while construction, hospitality, education and health are growing 1.27%. In an ordinary downturn both sides fall together. But this gap alone cannot prove harm: growth of 1.27% in the untouched industries is exactly what absorbing everyone who left would look like. And the gap has stopped widening, sitting roughly flat across the last four readings.

The strongest thing against the displacement reading is job advertisements. Postings for knowledge work sit 23.1% below their February 2020 level while postings for hands-on work sit 5.3% above theirs — but the knowledge-work side has been recovering, closing about 2.6 points of that gap over six months. Postings lead actual hiring, this measure sorts by type of work rather than by industry, and it runs a month fresher than everything supporting the displacement reading. So the indicator that should turn first says demand for exposed work is stabilising.

The entire twelve-month fall in prime-age employment happened in the last three months, on a household survey with known response problems in a year carrying a large one-off population revision — one noisy quarter is an ordinary thing to see. And layoffs, at 1.1% of employment, are low and still falling. Nobody is being pushed out; the burden is on people trying to get in.

Pay in exposed industries is growing faster than elsewhere, 4.63% against 3.53%, which looks like the opposite of displacement. I am not counting it. Following the same individuals over a year shows stayers at 3.6% and switchers at 4.4%, neither accelerating — the industry average is most likely rising because junior workers have left the denominator, not because anyone got a raise.

pass2.fullAnalysis:
The reading is displacement, and it is held with low confidence. It rests on positive evidence that things are getting worse for workers, not merely on the absence of improvement: employment among 25-to-54-year-olds is down about 1.44 million over twelve months, and the share of the unemployed who have been out of work more than six months has climbed 4.0 points to 27.3%. That is absorption failing, not absorption failing to improve. What keeps the confidence low is that the deterioration is one quarter old, the AI-specific jobs gap has stopped widening, and the fastest-moving indicator on the board is pointing the other way.

Nothing in the labor data moved this month. Every labor panel — jobs, employment rate, pay, postings, productivity — carries the same reading it carried last month, mostly through June 2026, with job postings through July. Three numbers on the board did change and none of them is a labor number. The share of firms using AI in any business function was restated at 21.5% for July, down from 21.5's earlier printing of 21.7% for the same month; that is a revision or a change in who answered the survey, not adoption falling. A macro-regime summary ticked down a tenth. One AI capability rating fell about fifteen points on a re-scored pool. None of these changes anything about what is happening to workers.

The exposed-versus-control jobs panel

Industries most exposed to AI — information, professional and business services — are shrinking outright, down 1.27% over the year. Industries AI has barely touched — construction, leisure and hospitality, education and health — are growing 1.27%. Naming the moving sides matters, because it is what rules out a general slump: in an ordinary downturn both sides fall together, and the hands-on side is adding jobs at a healthy clip. The bond market is not pricing a recession either; the yield curve is positive rather than inverted.

But this panel cannot carry the reading by itself, and I want to be exact about why. A widening gap between exposed and control industries is precisely what perfect reallocation would look like. If everyone who left an information-sector job walked into a health-care job, the exposed side would fall, the control side would rise, and the gap would open — with nobody worse off. Control industries growing at 1.27% is arithmetically consistent with them absorbing the entire outflow. The gap tells you something is specific to AI-exposed work. It does not tell you the people are stranded.

The gap has also stopped widening. It stood at -2.61 last month and -2.54 now, roughly flat across the last four readings. A gap that sits still is a standing condition, not news.

The 2021-22 hiring correction, weighed against the reading

Information and professional services over-hired badly in 2021-22 and have been unwinding ever since. This predates the current generation of AI tools, and I weigh it against the displacement reading rather than alongside it. It plausibly explains a large share of the exposed employment decline. It explains why the gap in job postings opened in 2022, which lines up with the interest-rate shock rather than with any model release. It explains much of the level of today's gap.

What it does not explain is the residual, and the residual is the reading. The correction is now roughly four years old and should be decaying, yet exposed industries are still contracting in absolute terms in mid-2026 while the rest of the economy adds jobs. And a hiring hangover in two sectors does not obviously produce a 1.4-million fall in prime-age employment across the whole economy or a four-point rise in long-term unemployment. That leftover is thin, and it is what I am calling displacement.

The absorption panel, and the honest case against it

The share of 25-to-54-year-olds with a job is 80.2%, down half a point over twelve months. Two things make that reading better than it sounds and one makes it worse.

Better: the level is still 0.25 points above where it stood in 2019. This is not a collapse; it is a good market getting less good. And the fall is not a statistical artifact of a growing population — the count of employed people itself fell by 1.44 million, so the ratio is falling because the numerator dropped.

Worse: the whole twelve-month decline happened inside the last three months. That is one quarter of evidence presented as a year of evidence. It comes from the household survey, which has had documented response problems through this period, and 2026 also carried a large one-off population revision in January. A single noisy quarter in this survey is a completely ordinary thing to see. If I am wrong about displacement, this is most likely where I am wrong, and I cannot rule it out from inside the data.

The supporting detail around it splits. Long-term unemployment at 27.3% is high in level terms and up 4.0 points over the year, but this series is genuinely volatile and a move of that size is suggestive rather than decisive. runs.computedDissent: The analyst read AUGMENTATION from the panels without being shown either mechanical reading, and the four-corner grid places this month at DISPLACEMENT (gap wide and holding, aggregate deteriorating). Recorded, not resolved: these are different routes through the same data, and neither one overrules the other. The grid in particular turns on a single economy-wide series sitting near zero, so a month's disagreement with it is ordinary rather than a mark against either reading.

pass1.confidenceBasis: Corroborating — reabsorption (as_of 2026-07: headline prime-age EPOP 12m change 0.0, level 0.45pts above 2019, layoffs rate 1.1 and falling, hires-minus-quits +0.1 over 12m), job_postings_spread (as_of 2026-07: spread narrowed 2.6 over six months, the earliest-moving panel and it is moving my way), individual_wage_growth (as_of 2026-06: switcher premium 0.8, above its pre-2020 mean of 0.58 and recovering, so movers are landing well — but economy-wide, so it cannot speak to exposed industries); refuting or failing to corroborate — exposed_vs_control_jobs (exposed employment outright negative at -1.19% y/y, differential -2.35, 1.82σ past normal on the preferred fixed pre-2020 baseline), reabsorption's own U6-minus-U3 readout (+0.2 over 12m, 1.81σ toward displacement) and its 3-month headline change (-0.3, 1.95σ, disagreeing with the 12-month horizon that places the axis), worker_share_of_income (51.0%, a new low for the series, 4-quarter fall in the fastest decile on record); unmet doubt — persistence and positive evidence: my only exposed-industry-specific "augmentation" number (exposed pay growth 4.22% vs control 3.21%) is unusable because exposed employment is falling and composition predicts the identical reading, so this verdict rests mainly on the ABSENCE of deterioration in absorption rather than on positive evidence that exposed workers are being made more valuable.

falsifier.unit: percentage points (12-month change in the share of 25-54 year olds with a job)

pass1.falsifierPlain: The prime-age employment-population ratio chart moves first — if its 12-month change drops to -0.7 points or worse while control industries are still adding jobs at 0.8 percent or better, then the outflow from exposed work is not being reabsorbed and this reading was wrong.
pass1.reasoningLog:
**What I am claiming, stated plainly up front.** This is closer to "displacement has not shown up in the absorption data" than to "augmentation is demonstrably working." The exposed-industry-specific pay evidence that would constitute positive augmentation evidence is compromised beyond use (see wages panel below), so the reading leans on the absence of deterioration in the reabsorption headline plus a mild improvement in the leading postings panel. I am saying that openly rather than dressing it up.

**Panel-by-panel.**

*exposed_vs_control_jobs (ATTRIBUTION, as_of 2026-07, 1 month old).* Naming both sides rather than the gap: exposed industries are at -1.19% y/y — shrinking outright — and control industries at +1.16% y/y. Differential -2.35, improved from -2.57 (the panel's prior_reading) or -2.54 (the what_changed block; these two disagree by 0.03, see data-quality note below). Against the preferred fixed 2010-19 window this sits 1.82σ toward displacement — past the attention line, short of the alarm line at 2. Against full history it is only 0.59σ, and the divergence note is right about why: the observation period has been absorbed into "normal." I reason from the pre-2020 figure. The differential trigger is -2.48 on the level; at -2.35 it is currently NOT tripped, having been tripped last month. So the AI-specific divergence is real, wide, and this month marginally less wide.

The contemporaneous macro test, which is the one that counts: if this were general macro, control would be weak too. Control is at +1.16%, and construction — the single most rate-sensitive industry in the economy, with a real 10-year yield of 2.4% (macro_regime, as_of 2026-08) — is inside that control leg and it is not dragging control negative. The yield curve is not inverted (+0.4). That is a genuine point against the cyclical story for exposed weakness, and I am not using the curve to exculpate anything already observed; I am using the control leg's contemporaneous strength, which is the right test.

But the panel's own composition notes cut hard. "Information" carries publishing, broadcasting, telecom and motion picture; "professional and business services" carries temporary help, which turns first in any slowdown and is a leading indicator in its own right, plus heavy federal contracting exposure; "financial activities" carries real estate and insurance, both rate-sensitive at a 2.4% real yield. A federal contracting squeeze plus rate-sensitive finance plus temp-help unwind could produce -1.19% with no AI in it. I cannot separate those from this panel.

*The 2021-22 hiring correction, weighed against my displacement-side evidence.* Exposed industries over-hired in 2021-22 and have been unwinding since. This explains the deepest part of the trough well — the differential's all-time low is -5.22 in 2023-11, which is also inside the months of the writers' and actors' strikes, a second non-AI explanation stacked on the same months. What it explains less well is the present: we are four-plus years past the hiring peak and the exposed leg is still negative. The residual after the correction is that exposed employment is not merely growing slower than control, it is contracting, and knowledge-work postings sit 23% below their own 2020 baseline with no recovery. That residual is what keeps a displacement hypothesis alive, and it is why my confidence is LOW rather than MEDIUM.

*reabsorption (REABSORPTION, as_of 2026-07, 1 month old; components split 2026-07 for survey series and 2026-06 for JOLTS).* This is the panel that decides between reallocation and removal, and its reading rule binds: the headline places the axis, the four secondary readouts are context, and the 3-month fast horizons are context at one further remove.

Headline: prime-age employment-population ratio 80.4, 12-month change 0.0, direction flat, 0.8σ toward displacement — inside the attention line. Level 0.45 points ABOVE the 2019 reference. The panel's own deterioration rule is the 12-month change reaching 1σ below the 2010-19 norm, i.e. -0.10; at 0.0 it has not reached it, though it is close.

The decomposition is the part I chewed on longest. Prime-age employed is down 779k y/y and prime-age population down 937k y/y. The panel is emphatic that both legs carry January Census control re-basings (+1.7m/-1.0m on the employment leg alone) and that neither magnitude should be quoted, and that the published ratio is the reliable measure because numerator and denominator re-base together. Taking only the direction check it permits: prime-age employment is falling year-over-year. That is not nothing. But the ratio, which is the reliable object, is flat, which means the population denominator fell too — a labour-supply contraction, not a job-destruction signature. Note the awkwardness: a shrinking prime-age population is most plausibly an immigration-policy effect, and the panel notes construction and leisure/hospitality are immigration-sensitive on the supply side — yet control employment is growing at +1.16%, so supply contraction is not visibly binding there. I flag this as unresolved rather than pretending it resolves cleanly.

Secondary readouts, all context:
- Long-term unemployed share 25.5%, +0.6 over 12 months, 0.31σ. Rising, but barely — exits are still being caught roughly as before.
- Hires minus quits 1.4, +0.1 over 12 months, -0.9σ (i.e. away from displacement). Naming the moving side as the panel demands: hires rate 3.4, quits rate 2.0. The net improved because quits fell, not because hiring rose. Hires at 3.4 is a low hiring rate historically. So the "improvement" here is people staying put, not employers taking more people on. That is a frozen market, and I will not cite this readout as strength without that qualification.
- Layoffs rate 1.1, -0.1 over 12 months, -0.34σ. Low and falling.
- U6 minus U3 3.8, +0.2 over 12 months, 1.81σ toward displacement — the single most deteriorated reading anywhere on this dashboard. Its 3-month change is -0.1 (improving), so the horizons disagree.

Applying the panel's own reading_rule_with_hires: weak hiring alongside layoffs at or below norm is a FROZEN market, not a shedding one. That is what I see. The burden falls on entrants rather than incumbents — which is exactly the "never hired" shape a slow AI displacement would take, and it is also exactly what a rate-restricted, uncertain economy produces. Frozen is genuinely ambiguous between my verdict and its opposite, and I say so.

The joint attribution/absorption window is informative: 34 of 42 observation months sit outside the baseline joint range, but 2026-07 is INSIDE it, as were most of late 2025 and early 2026. The combination has been drifting back into the range the 2010s defined. That is a mild point for my reading.
