Flat means the rest of the economy is precisely offsetting the exposed-side contraction, not absorbing it with room to spare.

Two panels that might have supplied positive evidence for augmentation do not.

Pay in AI-heavy industries is growing faster than in the industries AI has barely touched — 4.22% against 3.21% over the past year. That is backwards from what you would expect if AI were replacing these workers, and it is tempting. I do not lean on it, because employment in those same industries is falling. If entry-level hiring in software, consulting and finance has stopped, the remaining workforce skews senior and the average wage rises with nobody getting a raise, simply because the juniors left the denominator. Meanwhile the control group contains leisure and hospitality, low-paid and growing, dragging its average down from the other end. A junior-hiring collapse would produce this exact number. The panel cannot tell the two apart.

The check on that is a tracker that follows the same individuals twelve months apart, so changes in who is employed cannot move it. It says switchers are getting 4.4% and stayers 3.6%, both comfortably above the 2.3% inflation rate the market expects, and the switching premium is slightly better than its pre-2020 norm. On the national median, people who move jobs are landing at real pay gains. But this is an economy-wide measure and cannot be split into AI-exposed and everything else. A healthy national switching premium is entirely compatible with displaced knowledge workers taking pay cuts, and because it is a median it would miss a collapse concentrated in a minority. So the composition question on exposed-industry pay is unresolved, not resolved in favour of the augmentation reading.

The second failure is productivity. If AI were making exposed workers materially more productive at any scale, national productivity is where it should eventually show up. It is running at 2.2%, down from 2.9% the previous quarter. That is still respectable and above the 2010s average, but it decelerated, and I cannot claim augmentation is working on the back of a number that is slowing. It is economy-wide, so it can never attribute anything to AI specifically, and gains being absent is also consistent with the technology simply being too new to register in aggregate statistics. Either way, the positive case is not there.

The hardest piece of evidence against this reading is labour's share of national income. It has fallen to 51.0%, below any level in the history of the series, its fourth consecutive quarterly decline, down a full point over the past year. This series has drifted downward for fifty years, but at roughly a tenth of a point per year — the past year has run about seven times that pace. Declines this fast have happened before, in 2009 and 2010, and those were recessions. There is no recession here: control industries are growing, layoffs are low and falling, the yield curve is not inverted. A labour-share collapse outside a downturn is genuinely unusual and it is the observation I am least able to explain away.

Three things stop it moving the verdict, and readers should weigh them for themselves. It covers the whole economy, so it cannot be evidence about AI-exposed work specifically. It has been falling since the 1970s for reasons that predate AI by decades. And it is an accounting ratio whose other side is corporate profits, which move on margins, taxes and capital income without anyone losing a job. There is a fourth thing, and it cuts the other way: this is the oldest substantive number on the dashboard, from March 2026, when the employment panels run through July and postings through August. The single strongest piece of evidence against the augmentation reading is four to five months staler than the evidence for it, which means it could not yet reflect a turn in either direction. The June quarter print is the one to see.

Two smaller items. AI adoption keeps rising: 21.8% of firms report using it in some business function, up from 17.3% last November, and 41.5% among firms with 250 or more employees against 21.9% among the smallest. That removes the objection that the tools are not out there yet. It supplies no mechanism — the survey never asks whether any use made a role redundant. What would change the augmentation reading: the prime-age employment rate falling by six-tenths of a point or more over twelve months, while the control industries are still adding jobs at 0.8% or better. Both parts matter. The first says the labour market has stopped absorbing people. The second rules out a general recession as the explanation, since a downturn would drag construction, hospitality and health care down alongside everything else. Together they describe a labour market that stopped absorbing without a general contraction to blame, which is what this reading being wrong looks like. falsifier.unit: percentage points (12-month change in 25-54 employment-to-population ratio)

runs.falsifierPlain: This reading is overturned if the prime-age employment ratio's 12-month change drops to -0.62 points or worse (its own 2-sigma deterioration line) while the exposed-minus-control jobs gap also reaches -2.48 or worse, showing exposed workers failing to land elsewhere rather than merely moving.

pairedState.reading: AI-exposed work is diverging AND the aggregate is deteriorating, so the outflow is not landing.

definitions.widening: the exposed-minus-control job-growth gap is at least 0 standard deviation further below its 2010-01..2019-12 average, that window fixed and never rolling, AND has been for 3 consecutive readings. The run requirement is the newer half and it is what stops the vertical axis deciding this grid on its own: one month past the line used to establish this axis, the gap has been past the line since 2023, and the result was that the only thing ever changing the quadrant was an economy-wide employment change that an ordinary recession moves
definitions.deteriorating: the prime-age (25-54) employment-population ratio is LOWER than it was twelve months ago. A change against raw zero, with no baseline, no reference year and no threshold, because those were all the wrong kind of answer here: a level against 2019 anchored the boundary to a cyclical peak and would have read displacement across most of the 2010s, and z-scoring the change against 2010-2019 scored a mature expansion against a decade of recovery. Zero involves no distribution, so nothing can contaminate it.

definitions.deteriorating: the prime-age (25-54) employment-population ratio is LOWER than it was twelve months ago. A change against raw zero, with no baseline, no reference year and no threshold, because those were all the wrong kind of answer here: a level against 2019 anchored the boundary to a cyclical peak and would have read displacement across most of the 2010s, and z-scoring the change against 2010-2019 scored a mature expansion against a decade of recovery. Zero involves no distribution, so nothing can contaminate it.

path.lineRationale: Both axes cross at zero, and zero is a fact about each measure rather than a chosen threshold: the gap sitting at its own 2010s norm, and employment flat year-over-year. Validated before adoption — this never calls the 2014-2019 boom displacement.

runs.computedDissent: The analyst read AUGMENTATION from the panels without being shown either mechanical reading, and the four-corner grid places this month at DISPLACEMENT (gap wide and holding, aggregate deteriorating). Recorded, not resolved: these are different routes through the same data, and neither one overrules the other. The grid in particular turns on a single economy-wide series sitting near zero, so a month's disagreement with it is ordinary rather than a mark against either reading.

pass1.confidenceBasis: Corroborating: reabsorption headline (prime-age employment ratio, LNS12300060, as_of 2026-07) is flat over 12 months and above its 2019 level, and its JOLTS-based components (hires-minus-quits rising, layoffs falling) — a genuinely different source from the CPS headline — agree the market is not shedding people; job_postings_spread's 6-month change is narrowing rather than widening. Refuting / uncorroborated: exposed_vs_control_jobs has sat past its attention line for the last four readings without closing, the underemployment gap secondary readout is at 1.81σ (close to its alarm line), and the exposed-vs-control wage gap is confounded by falling exposed headcount so it cannot be read at face value. Unmet doubt: the calm reading leans partly on correlated CPS-sourced components (headline + long-term-unemployed share) rather than fully independent confirmation, and the flat 12-month headline sits beside a falling 3-month fast_horizon (agrees_with_headline: false) that could be an early turn the 12-month figure can't show yet.

falsifier.unit: percentage points (12-month change in 25-54 employment-to-population ratio)

pass1.falsifierPlain: This reading is overturned if the prime-age employment ratio's 12-month change drops to -0.62 points or worse (its own 2-sigma deterioration line) while the exposed-minus-control jobs gap also reaches -2.48 or worse, showing exposed workers failing to land elsewhere rather than merely moving.
pass1.reasoningLog:
POPULATIONS FIRST. Three groups appear here and I've tried not to mix them: exposed industries (information/prof-biz/financial — the exposed_vs_control_jobs and exposed_vs_control_wages panels, and the occupation-cut job_postings_spread), control industries (construction/leisure-hospitality/education-health — same two panels), and economy-wide series (labor_productivity, worker_share_of_income, individual_wage_growth, ai_adoption, macro_regime, all capability panels). The BLS ground-truth payroll figure in the news package (-23k month-over-month, all-nonfarm) is economy-wide and I have not paired it against an exposed-industry number as if they measured the same thing.

PANEL BY PANEL

labor_productivity (GAINS_TEST, economy-wide, as_of 2026-06, 2 months old). Latest 2.2%, down from 2.9% the prior quarter, one quarter below the 2.7 "internet-boom" lower band. Against the clean pre-2020 baseline (mean 1.27, sd 1.12) this is still comfortably above average — roughly +0.8σ — so it is not collapsed, just decelerating from an elevated reading. Per its own panel_role this is a check on whether augmentation gains are visible at all, not evidence for or against displacement, and it cannot be attributed to AI-exposed work since it's economy-wide. Inversion: someone arguing displacement could point to the deceleration (2.9→2.2) as gains fading just as adoption rises, which would undercut a "gains are coming" augmentation story — but the panel's own role note says absence of gains is equally consistent with the technology being too new to register, so I treat this as inconclusive context, not support for either verdict.

exposed_vs_control_jobs (ATTRIBUTION, as_of 2026-07, 1 month old). Exposed employment -1.19% YoY, control +1.16% YoY, differential -2.35, essentially unchanged from -2.57 last month and "holding roughly flat over the last 4 readings." Against the fixed pre-2020 baseline this is 1.82σ toward displacement — past the attention line (1) but short of the alarm line (2) and short of the stated attribution trigger (-2.48). The panel's own measurement_artifact is explicit that this measures reallocation, not destruction, and that perfect reallocation with everybody re-employed produces the maximally negative reading — so a stalled negative gap is not on its own evidence of harm. Inversion (steelmanning displacement): a gap that has been past the attention line for four straight readings without closing is also what a completed contraction that has settled at a new, permanently lower level of exposed employment would look like — "flat" cuts both ways, and I can't rule out that the reallocation already happened and simply isn't reversing. I weight this against my own verdict rather than pretending the stall is unambiguously reassuring.

reabsorption (REABSORPTION, headline as_of 2026-07, 1 month old — binds per its panel_role). Headline: 25-54 employment ratio 80.4%, 0.0 change over 12 months, 0.8σ toward displacement on the fixed baseline (below the 1σ attention line), and 0.45 points above its 2019 reference level. This is the panel that decides whether the exposed/control gap reflects destruction or reallocation, and its own reading rule states the 12-month change is decisive while the 3-month fast_horizon and the four secondary readouts are context. The 3-month horizon is falling (-0.3, 1.36σ against the preferred fixed baseline) and disagrees with the flat 12-month headline (agrees_with_headline: false) — I flag this openly as a possible early turn that the slower 12-month figure cannot yet show, rather than hiding it. Secondaries: long-term-unemployed share rising mildly (0.31σ, below attention); hires-minus-quits rising (+0.1 over 12mo, -0.9σ, i.e. healthy) from a genuinely different source (JOLTS, not CPS); layoffs falling (-0.34σ, healthy); underemployment gap (U6-U3) rising 0.2 pts over 12 months, 1.81σ toward displacement — the most concerning secondary, close to its alarm line, though its own 3-month horizon is falling (context only, disagreeing with its own 12-month direction). Taken together the decisive headline is flat/healthy, the independent JOLTS-based readouts (hires-minus-quits, layoffs) are healthy, and only the underemployment gap and long-term-unemployment share lean mildly toward deterioration. Per the panel's own weighting rule ("if the gap is widening while prime-age employment, long-term unemployment and hiring hold steady, workers are moving rather than being removed") this is the panel that keeps me off a displacement verdict. Inversion: I could be over-trusting a flat headline that is itself built on a survey (CPS) whose January control-population rebasing the panel's own decomposition note flags as contaminating any 12-month household-survey comparison — though the note is explicit that the ratio itself (unlike the levels beneath it) is not distorted by that rebasing, so I don't think this undermines the headline specifically, just the level components beneath it, which I have not quoted.

exposed_vs_control_wages (ATTRIBUTION, as_of 2026-07, 1 month old). Exposed pay +4.22% YoY vs control +3.21%, differential +1.00, widened slightly from +0.93. Per the panel's own weighting rule, because exposed employment is currently falling (-1.19% YoY, confirmed by the jobs panel), a composition story (juniors leaving the denominator, seniors remaining) and a genuine "AI is bidding up the workers who remain" story predict the identical observation, so this panel cannot referee between augmentation and displacement by itself. I read it as inconclusive rather than at face value.

individual_wage_growth (COMPOSITION_CONTROL, economy-wide, as_of 2026-07, 1 month old). Job stayers +3.6%, switchers +4.4%, switcher premium 0.8, unchanged from last month and only -0.54σ against the fixed baseline (i.e., close to normal, if anything slightly below the typical switcher premium, not accelerating). This is the composition-immune check for the wage panel above: if exposed pay were genuinely accelerating for AI-related reasons I might expect the switcher premium (which captures people moving toward better-paying work) to be unusually elevated, and it is not — it's within its ordinary range. This doesn't prove the exposed-wage acceleration is pure composition (this series is economy-wide and can't be cut to exposed industries), but it removes one piece of positive evidence I might otherwise have leaned on for an "augmentation is paying exposed workers more" story. I am treating the wage evidence overall as too confounded to count as positive support for augmentation, consistent with the prompt's insistence that absence-of-deterioration is not the same claim as positive value-creation.

job_postings_spread (ATTRIBUTION, occupation-cut, as_of 2026-08, the freshest panel, and per its own role note the earliest-moving of the three attribution panels). Levels: exposed knowledge-work postings sit 23.2% below their own Feb-2020 level; control hands-on postings sit 4.7% above theirs — naming both sides rather than just the spread. The level is dominated by a 2022 rate-driven contraction per the panel's own measurement_artifact (interest-rate timing, not AI-release timing), so per its own weighting rule I read the change, not the level: spread_change_over_6_months is +3.7 (narrowing) and the most recent month also narrowed slightly (-28.4 → -27.9). I cannot tell from the data which side moved to produce that narrowing — I only have current levels, not the levels six months back broken out by side — so I'm treating "narrowing" as a mild, uncertain positive rather than a confirmed recovery. Inversion: a skeptic could argue a 0.8-point monthly wiggle inside a spread that has been "roughly flat since 2022" is noise, and that the level (-23.2% for exposed, deeply negative for nearly four years) is the real story regardless of what the panel's own weighting rule says to privilege — I think the weighting rule is right that the level is mostly a legacy 2022 event, but I'm not leaning hard on the narrowing either; it's weak support, stated as weak.

macro_regime / contemporaneous test on controls. pass2.publishedNote:
The reading stays on augmentation this month, but that word means displacement has not shown up in the data yet — it is not a finding that AI is visibly making exposed workers more valuable. That distinction matters because the positive case, that exposed workers are being paid more for genuinely more productive work, remains too tangled with other explanations to count as support on its own.

Almost nothing moved since last month. The one panel with fresh news is job postings: postings for knowledge-work occupations most exposed to AI, which have sat roughly 23% below their pre-2020 level for years, narrowed their gap with hands-on control occupations slightly, from 28.7 points behind to 27.9 points behind. That is a small, ambiguous wobble inside a spread that has been roughly flat since a 2022 contraction, not a turn. Every other panel — hiring, wages, productivity, adoption — is unchanged from a month ago.

The strongest thing keeping this call at augmentation is the prime-age employment picture: the share of 25-54 year-olds employed sits at 80.4%, unchanged over the past year and still above its pre-pandemic level, while a separate measure of hiring versus quits shows employers hiring faster than workers are quitting, with layoffs falling. If AI were actively pushing workers out of exposed industries and they were failing to land elsewhere, this is the kind of measure that would break down first, and it has not.

The strongest thing cutting against it is that AI-exposed industries — information, professional and business services, financial activities — have been shrinking for months, down 1.19% over the past year, while non-exposed industries — construction, leisure and hospitality, education and health — are growing, up 1.16%. That gap has sat past the point of concern for four straight monthly readings without closing. A gap that persists this long without narrowing is also consistent with a story where the reallocation already happened and simply is not reversing: a smaller exposed workforce that has settled at a new, lower level, rather than one still finding its way to new jobs. Separately, a broader measure of underemployment is rising and closing in on its own concerning level, and the faster three-month read on the prime-age employment ratio is falling even though the slower twelve-month figure this whole call rests on is still flat — a possible early crack the calmer number cannot show yet.

What to watch: the prime-age employment ratio on the reabsorption panel, specifically whether its three-month trend keeps falling into the twelve-month figure, since that slower number is the one this entire call is built on.
pass2.fullAnalysis:
The call is augmentation, unchanged from last month, and it needs to be read carefully: this is a finding that displacement has not shown up in the data, not a finding that AI is visibly making exposed workers more productive or better paid. The two are different claims, and the evidence here only supports the first one.

Three groups of workers appear in this analysis and they should not be blurred together. Exposed industries are information, professional and business services, and financial activities — the sectors most exposed to AI tools. Control industries are construction, leisure and hospitality, and education and health — sectors with much less AI exposure, used as a comparison group. A third set of measures is economy-wide and does not distinguish between the two: overall productivity, overall wage growth by job-switching status, the labor share of income, and the pace of AI adoption across all firms. Mixing these up is the single easiest way to over-read this kind of data, so every number below is labeled with which group it describes.

What changed this month: almost nothing. Of the panels tracked, only one moved at all. Job postings for the occupations most exposed to AI — the kind of knowledge work AI tools target most directly — sit about 23% below their pre-2020 level, a gap dominated by a 2022 interest-rate-driven contraction rather than anything AI-specific. That gap narrowed slightly this month, from 28.7 points behind hands-on control occupations to 27.9 points behind. It is a small move inside a spread that has been roughly flat for years, and there is no way to tell from this figure alone which side — exposed postings recovering, or control postings cooling — produced the narrowing. It counts as weak, uncertain support for augmentation, stated as weak. Every other panel is unchanged from last month's reading.

The strongest evidence supporting the augmentation call is the prime-age employment picture. The share of 25-54 year-olds employed sits at 80.4%, unchanged over the past twelve months and still above its pre-pandemic level. This is the measure that decides whether the weakness visible in exposed industries is workers being pushed out and left stranded, or workers moving to different jobs. A separate, independently sourced measure — job openings data showing hiring outpacing quits, and a falling layoff rate — points the same healthy direction. If AI-driven displacement were underway and workers were failing to land elsewhere, this is where it would first appear as a broad break, and it has not appeared.

The strongest evidence against the call, and the one that most needs to be said plainly rather than softened, is that the gap between exposed and control industries has not closed. Exposed-industry employment fell 1.19% over the past year while control-industry employment grew 1.16% — a specific, industry-linked divergence, confirmed by checking that control industries are not weak for unrelated macro reasons (they are not; if the economy overall were sliding, both groups would be weak, and only one is). That divergence has now sat past the level that would normally draw attention for four consecutive monthly readings without narrowing. A gap that persists this long without closing is also exactly what you would see if the reallocation had already happened and simply settled at a new, lower level of exposed employment — workers who left these industries not finding their way back, rather than being in the process of finding new jobs. The data available cannot distinguish "moving, but slowly" from "already displaced, and the level has just stopped falling further." Two more things nudge in the same worrying direction: a broader measure of underemployment — workers stuck in part-time jobs who want full-time work — has been rising and is closing in on its own concern level, and the faster three-month read on the prime-age employment ratio is falling even though the twelve-month figure the whole call rests on is still flat. That is a live disagreement between a fast-moving and a slow-moving version of the same underlying measure, and it is not resolved.

Other panels add texture but do not move the call. Economy-wide productivity growth slowed to 2.2% from 2.9% the prior quarter — still historically decent, but decelerating right as AI adoption rises, which is inconclusive on its own since the technology could simply be too new to show up either way. Pay in AI-exposed industries is growing faster than in control industries, 4.22% against 3.21%, which sounds like a positive augmentation signal, but because exposed employment is shrinking at the same time, a much less flattering explanation fits the same numbers equally well: junior, lower-paid workers leaving the exposed workforce while higher-paid, more senior workers remain, mechanically pulling the average up with no productivity story required. An economy-wide check on whether people who switch jobs are commanding better pay right now — a measure immune to that same composition problem — shows nothing unusual, which removes one piece of evidence that might otherwise have supported a genuine augmentation story. AI adoption among firms is real and growing, from 17.3% to 21.8% of firms over nine months, with much heavier adoption at large firms, but adoption data cannot link any specific firm's AI use to that firm's hiring decisions, so it establishes only that the precondition for displacement exists, not that displacement is happening. A separate measure of the labor share of national income going to workers fell at one of the faster rates seen in decades of data, but slower than in the 2008 and 2010 recessions, and it is over five months old, so it is treated as background rather than current evidence. NOTIFICATION: Reading holds: augmentation. Only mover was postings gap narrowing slightly this month.
TAGLINE: Stalled gap, quiet month
FULL_ANALYSIS:
The call is augmentation, unchanged from last month, and it needs to be read carefully: this is a finding that displacement has not shown up in the data, not a finding that AI is visibly making exposed workers more productive or better paid. The two are different claims, and the evidence here only supports the first one.

Three groups of workers appear in this analysis and they should not be blurred together. Exposed industries are information, professional and business services, and financial activities — the sectors most exposed to AI tools. Control industries are construction, leisure and hospitality, and education and health — sectors with much less AI exposure, used as a comparison group. A third set of measures is economy-wide and does not distinguish between the two: overall productivity, overall wage growth by job-switching status, the labor share of income, and the pace of AI adoption across all firms. Mixing these up is the single easiest way to over-read this kind of data, so every number below is labeled with which group it describes.

What changed this month: almost nothing. Of the panels tracked, only one moved at all. Job postings for the occupations most exposed to AI — the kind of knowledge work AI tools target most directly — sit about 23% below their pre-2020 level, a gap dominated by a 2022 interest-rate-driven contraction rather than anything AI-specific. That gap narrowed slightly this month, from 28.7 points behind hands-on control occupations to 27.9 points behind. It is a small move inside a spread that has been roughly flat for years, and there is no way to tell from this figure alone which side — exposed postings recovering, or control postings cooling — produced the narrowing. It counts as weak, uncertain support for augmentation, stated as weak. Every other panel is unchanged from last month's reading.

The strongest evidence supporting the augmentation call is the prime-age employment picture. The share of 25-54 year-olds employed sits at 80.4%, unchanged over the past twelve months and still above its pre-pandemic level. This is the measure that decides whether the weakness visible in exposed industries is workers being pushed out and left stranded, or workers moving to different jobs. A separate, independently sourced measure — job openings data showing hiring outpacing quits, and a falling layoff rate — points the same healthy direction. If AI-driven displacement were underway and workers were failing to land elsewhere, this is where it would first appear as a broad break, and it has not appeared.

The strongest evidence against the call, and the one that most needs to be said plainly rather than softened, is that the gap between exposed and control industries has not closed. Exposed-industry employment fell 1.19% over the past year while control-industry employment grew 1.16% — a specific, industry-linked divergence, confirmed by checking that control industries are not weak for unrelated macro reasons (they are not; if the economy overall were sliding, both groups would be weak, and only one is). That divergence has now sat past the level that would normally draw attention for four consecutive monthly readings without narrowing. A gap that persists this long without closing is also exactly what you would see if the reallocation had already happened and simply settled at a new, lower level of exposed employment — workers who left these industries not finding their way back, rather than being in the process of finding new jobs. The data available cannot distinguish "moving, but slowly" from "already displaced, and the level has just stopped falling further." Two more things nudge in the same worrying direction: a broader measure of underemployment — workers stuck in part-time jobs who want full-time work — has been rising and is closing in on its own concern level, and the faster three-month read on the prime-age employment ratio is falling even though the twelve-month figure the whole call rests on is still flat. That is a live disagreement between a fast-moving and a slow-moving version of the same underlying measure, and it is not resolved.

Other panels add texture but do not move the call. Economy-wide productivity growth slowed to 2.2% from 2.9% the prior quarter — still historically decent, but decelerating right as AI adoption rises, which is inconclusive on its own since the technology could simply be too new to show up either way. Pay in AI-exposed industries is growing faster than in control industries, 4.22% against 3.21%, which sounds like a positive augmentation signal, but because exposed employment is shrinking at the same time, a much less flattering explanation fits the same numbers equally well: junior, lower-paid workers leaving the exposed workforce while higher-paid, more senior workers remain, mechanically pulling the average up with no productivity story required. An economy-wide check on whether people who switch jobs are commanding better pay right now — a measure immune to that same composition problem — shows nothing unusual, which removes one piece of evidence that might otherwise have supported a genuine augmentation story. AI adoption among firms is real and growing, from 17.3% to 21.8% of firms over nine months, with much heavier adoption at large firms, but adoption data cannot link any specific firm's AI use to that firm's hiring decisions, so it establishes only that the precondition for displacement exists, not that displacement is happening. A separate measure of the labor share of national income going to workers fell at one of the faster rates seen in decades of data, but slower than in the 2008 and 2010 recessions, and it is over five months old, so it is treated as background rather than current evidence. Frontier AI capability benchmarks continue to improve, but no measure here connects a benchmark score to an employment outcome, so they are read for context only and are not allowed to tip the labor call either way.

This reading would flip if two things happened together: the prime-age employment ratio's twelve-month change would need to drop substantially below flat — a real, sustained deterioration rather than ordinary month-to-month noise — while the exposed-versus-control jobs gap also widens further into genuinely alarming territory. Requiring both together matters: an ordinary broad economic slowdown would tend to weaken control industries too and narrow that second gap, not widen it, so the combination is what would separate real AI-linked displacement from an unrelated downturn. Neither condition is close to firing yet, but the exposed-jobs gap is closer to its concerning level than the employment ratio is, and both series update monthly, so there is a real chance to see this move one way or the other within the next few months.

PUBLISHED_NOTE:
The reading stays on augmentation this month, but that word means displacement has not shown up in the data yet — it is not a finding that AI is visibly making exposed workers more valuable. That distinction matters because the positive case, that exposed workers are being paid more for genuinely more productive work, remains too tangled with other explanations to count as support on its own.

Almost nothing moved since last month. The one panel with fresh news is job postings: postings for knowledge-work occupations most exposed to AI, which have sat roughly 23% below their pre-2020 level for years, narrowed their gap with hands-on control occupations slightly, from 28.7 points behind to 27.9 points behind. That gap has sat past the point of concern for four straight monthly readings without closing. A gap that persists this long without narrowing is also consistent with a story where the reallocation already happened and simply is not reversing: a smaller exposed workforce that has settled at a new, lower level, rather than one still finding its way to new jobs. What to watch: the prime-age employment ratio on the reabsorption panel, specifically whether its three-month trend keeps falling into the twelve-month figure, since that slower number is the one this entire call is built on.

definitions.widening: the exposed-minus-control job-growth gap is at least 0 standard deviation further below its 2010-01..2019-12 average, that window fixed and never rolling, AND has been for 3 consecutive readings. The run requirement is the newer half and it is what stops the vertical axis deciding this grid on its own: one month past the line used to establish this axis, the gap has been past the line since 2023, and the result was that the only thing ever changing the quadrant was an economy-wide employment change that an ordinary recession moves
definitions.deteriorating: the prime-age (25-54) employment-population ratio is LOWER than it was twelve months ago. Zero involves no distribution, so nothing can contaminate it.

runs.computedDissent: The analyst read AUGMENTATION from the panels without being shown either mechanical reading, and the four-corner grid places this month at DISPLACEMENT (gap wide and holding, aggregate deteriorating). Recorded, not resolved: these are different routes through the same data, and neither one overrules the other. The grid in particular turns on a single economy-wide series sitting near zero, so a month's disagreement with it is ordinary rather than a mark against either reading.

pass1.confidenceBasis: Corroborating: reabsorption headline (LNS12300060, as_of 2026-07) flat at 0 over 12 months and 0.45pts above its 2019 level; secondary hires-minus-quits improving (+0.1 12m) and layoffs falling (-0.1 12m), i.e. not a shedding labor market. Refuting/weak: exposed_vs_control_jobs (as_of 2026-07) newly crossed its attention line (1.82σ vs fixed baseline) this reading, and the reabsorption headline's own 3-month fast horizon is falling (-0.3, 1.95σ, nearly at alarm) even though the rule says that horizon is context-only, not a vote. Unmet doubt: the signal I'm relying on (flat 12-month headline) is a trailing measure and could be masking a turn the faster horizon is already showing — I have not resolved that, which is why this stays LOW rather than MEDIUM.

pass1.falsifierPlain: This reading is overturned if the prime-age employment-population ratio's 12-month change (reabsorption headline) falls to -0.5 points or below while the exposed-minus-control jobs differential simultaneously falls to -2.48 or below, both inside the next 90 days.
pass1.reasoningLog:
Starting point: the dashboard's own architecture separates ATTRIBUTION (is something happening that's specific to AI-exposed work) from REABSORPTION (did the people who left land somewhere). I worked those two first because the panel notes are explicit that neither answers the verdict alone.

exposed_vs_control_jobs (as_of 2026-07): exposed YoY -1.19%, control +1.16%, differential -2.35, prior month -2.57. Deviation against the preferred fixed 2010-19 baseline is 1.82σ — past the attention line (1) but short of alarm (2), and the streak note says this crossing is NEW this reading even though the differential itself moved slightly toward zero month over month (from -2.57 to -2.35) and has been "roughly flat over the last 4 readings." That's a genuine internal tension in the panel worth flagging rather than smoothing over: the level newly crossed a line while itself improving slightly — likely an artifact of how the streak/deviation windows are computed rather than a real acceleration, and I did not lean on the "newly crossed" framing as if it meant fresh deterioration. Per its own measurement_artifact, this differential cannot distinguish destruction from reallocation, and per the industry_proxy_caveat, "information" includes strike- and streaming-exposed subsectors and "professional/business services" includes staffing, which leads ANY slowdown, AI or not. So I read this panel as establishing only: something is happening to exposed-coded industries, moderately past normal, not accelerating in the latest data. Inversion: the strongest opposite reading is that this is a plateau at an already-abnormal level rather than noise, i.e., a stalled-but-real divergence that the flat gap description is underselling — I address this by not treating "flat" as reassuring, only as "not yet escalating."

reabsorption (as_of 2026-07, mixed vintages: survey legs 2026-07, JOLTS legs 2026-06 — under one quarter apart, so comparable, but I note the gap explicitly per the vintage rule). Headline: prime-age employment-population ratio 12-month change = 0 (flat), and the level sits 0.45pts above the 2019 reference — this is the binding field per the panel's own reading_rule. The decomposition note is explicit that raw employment/population levels are contaminated by January control re-basing on BOTH legs, so I only used the ratio, not the levels, and did not compare the household-survey figure to the payroll headline in the news package (the panel itself forbids netting those). Secondary readouts, held as context per the panel's own rule: long-term unemployed share +0.6 12m (deviation 0.31, mild), hires-minus-quits +0.1 12m (deviation -0.9, i.e. away from displacement), layoffs -0.1 12m (deviation -0.34, away from displacement — layoffs are not elevated, which per the panel's own pairing rule with hiring rules out "cyclical shedding" as the story; hiring is not obviously frozen either since hires (3.4) sit comfortably above quits (2.0)). The one genuinely concerning secondary readout is the underemployment gap (U6-U3): +0.2 12m, deviation 1.81 against the fixed baseline — close to alarm — which is exactly the "landed but landed badly" signature the panel describes. But its own 3-month fast horizon is falling (-0.1), disagreeing with the 12-month figure, so the most recent quarter looks like it's easing rather than worsening. I read this as unresolved rather than confirmatory in either direction. Fast horizon on the headline itself (-0.3 over 3 months, 1.95σ) is the one piece of context I take most seriously as a possible early turn, but the panel's own rule ("CONTEXT ONLY... must not be treated as a second vote") means I cannot let it move the headline verdict — I instead used it to set my confidence at LOW and to build the overturn condition on the very next headline readings.

Put together: the attribution panel shows a real but non-escalating divergence; the reabsorption panel — which is what decides whether that divergence is displacement or reallocation — shows no aggregate deterioration on its binding field, with the one soft spot (underemployment) itself ambiguous on direction. Per the panel's own weighting rule ("if the gap is widening while absorption holds steady, workers are moving rather than being removed"), and given the gap is not clearly widening here, I read this as reallocation-not-yet-displacement, i.e., closer to "displacement not started" than to "displacement observed." I am stating explicitly that this rests mainly on the ABSENCE of deterioration (flat prime-age ratio, low layoffs, hires still ahead of quits) rather than on positive evidence that exposed workers are being made more valuable — so the correct label under the forced choice is AUGMENTATION, but with the caveat foregrounded rather than dressed up as a stronger claim.

exposed_vs_control_wages (as_of 2026-07): exposed pay +4.22% YoY vs control +3.21%, differential +1.00, rising from +0.93. On its face this differential favors exposed workers and could be read as augmentation (AI-adjacent workers commanding a growing premium). But the panel's own measurement_artifact is decisive here: exposed employment is FALLING (-1.19% YoY, per the jobs panel), and the weighting_rule states that when exposed employment is falling, a composition story (junior/lower-paid workers leaving the denominator, pulling the average up with nobody getting a raise) predicts exactly this same observation, so the panel "cannot separate them by itself." I checked the cross-check panel — individual_wage_growth (COMPOSITION_CONTROL, economy-wide, same-people basis): job stayers 3.6%, switchers 4.4%, switcher premium 0.8, essentially at its long-run fixed-baseline average (mean 0.58, sd 0.41 → about 0.5σ) and unchanged from the prior month. This is economy-wide so it cannot itself confirm or deny an exposed-industry story, but it gives no sign of an unusual, broad acceleration in switcher pay that would need to ride alongside a genuine exposed-industry pay story. Given that, I treat the exposed-vs-control wage differential as likely substantially composition-driven and I am NOT counting it as positive evidence for augmentation, consistent with the instruction not to quote an unresolved composition figure at face value. Inversion done: the strongest opposite reading (rising exposed pay = real augmentation) is the one I set aside for the composition reason above, stated in the panel's own terms (falling exposed employment + industry-average mechanics), not by citation of the panel_role label.

job_postings_spread (as_of 2026-08, freshest panel, earliest-moving per its own role): exposed occupations -23 vs own Feb-2020 baseline, control +4.6; spread -27.6, essentially flat vs -27.9 last month, and per its own measurement_artifact this spread opened in 2022 on the back of the tightening cycle (rate-sensitive white-collar hiring cut first), predating diffused AI use in hiring — so the LEVEL is substantially a stale 2022 event and I read only the CHANGE. Six-month change is +4 (spread narrowing, i.e., mild improvement on the exposed side relative to control) and the one-month change is +0.3. Both are small relative to the series' own full-history sd of 4.39, so I treat this as "not currently deteriorating further" rather than "recovering" — a weak, noisy signal that nonetheless does not contradict the reabsorption-based read. Inversion: since postings lead employment, a reader could argue this flatness is exactly the kind of thing that would turn first if a real deterioration were coming, and a single month's +0.3 tells us nothing about whether that turn is imminent — I accept that and it is part of why confidence stays LOW rather than moving up.

labor_productivity (GAINS_TEST, economy-wide, as_of 2026-06 — two months older than the July-dated exposed/reabsorption panels, noted per the vintage rule): 2.2%, down from 2.9%, now below the 2.7 "internet-boom" lower band for one quarter. This is explicitly a check on the AUGMENTATION story rather than on displacement (it's economy-wide and can't attribute to AI either way), and it argues against a strong positive augmentation claim — gains are not visibly accelerating in the aggregate, if anything decelerating. I used this to keep the verdict modest ("displacement not started" rather than "augmentation working") rather than to move it toward displacement, since panel_role explicitly says gains being absent is consistent with several things including simple technological immaturity, and it cannot speak to exposed-industry displacement.

ai_adoption: rising steadily (17.3%→21.8% since Nov 2025), concentrated more in larger firms (41.5% for 250+ vs 21.9% for the smallest band), so worker-level exposure is understated by the firm-count headline. This establishes that the deployment precondition for an AI-labor story is present and growing — it "removes an objection" to an AI-specific explanation existing at all, per its own panel note — but per the same note it carries no firm-level linkage to any layoff and cannot itself supply a labor-market finding. I used it only as background plausibility, not as evidence either way.

worker_share_of_income: economy-wide, declining for 40+ years, currently in the fastest 5% of 4-quarter declines on record, but the panel itself notes that ordinary recessions (2009, 2010) produced faster declines than this, and it explicitly cannot be attributed to AI. I read it as descriptive texture only, consistent with its DESCRIPTIVE role and its own no-threshold registration — a real move, but not specific to AI-exposed work and not usable as attribution.

ai_use_automation_vs_augmentation, ai_capability_metr, ai_capability_gdpval_ratings, ai_capability_vs_human_experts: all either stale (11 and 8 months old) or explicitly does_not_contribute. I read them for texture only — the automation/augmentation split (43/57) has been stable across releases but predates the current labor months by most of a year and is vendor-usage-based, not a labor measure; the capability panels show frontier models continuing to improve on clean benchmark tasks (up to ~186 minutes at 80% reliability, and GPT-5.2 Thinking clearing experts 70.9% of the time wins+ties, 49.7% wins-only i.e. near true parity) but none of that is an event in any worker's employment, so none of it moved the verdict, consistent with their panel_role.

macro_regime (as_of 2026-08): yield curve not inverted (10y-2y = +0.5), real 10yr yield 2.4%, expected inflation 2.3%. I did not use this to exculpate any weakness already in the data (the prompt is explicit the curve is forward-looking and cannot do that). Instead I ran the contemporaneous test the prompt asks for: control industries are growing at +1.16% YoY, i.e., healthy, which argues against a general macro slump being the story behind the exposed-industry softness — that softness looks more specific to the exposed codes than to the economy broadly, though I still can't cleanly separate "AI" from "media strikes / staffing-sector leading indicator / rate-sensitive finance" within those codes, which is exactly why I kept this reading at LOW rather than promoting it to a confident directional call.

News package: BLS ground truth for July shows payrolls -23k (essentially flat) and unemployment 4.1%, consistent with the flat reabsorption headline and not indicating a fresh air-pocket. The two AP wire pieces are generic macro texture (inflation, Iran, Fed, mortgage rates) with no specific mechanism tying them to AI-exposed industries specifically, so I set them aside — they could move rates or general sentiment but nothing in them explains why exposed pay/employment would move differently from control. The NY Fed "stock market participation and rate transmission" piece is about monetary-policy mechanics, not labor displacement, and I set it aside on the same grounds. The NY Fed "AI's Impact on Labor and Hiring" piece is the one on-topic item, but I have only the title, not tested content, and per the rules news generates hypotheses but never moves the verdict — I have nothing in it I can test against a series beyond what the dashboard panels themselves already carry, so it neither strengthens nor weakens my read; I note its existence rather than use it.

Rejected verdict: DISPLACEMENT. The case for it would need either the attribution panel to be escalating (it is not — flat/newly-at-attention rather than accelerating toward alarm) or the reabsorption headline to be deteriorating (it is flat, and its supporting hiring/layoffs legs are improving, not worsening). The strongest displacement-leaning fact — underemployment gap at 1.81σ — is undercut by its own 3-month easing, so I could not treat it as decisive.

Rejected verdict: CONFOUNDED. This is available only when a named cause fully explains an otherwise-displacement-shaped pattern. Here I am not reading a displacement-shaped pattern to begin with — the reabsorption panel that is supposed to decide that question shows no deterioration — so there is no positive displacement reading left for a confounder to explain away. The industry-proxy issues (strikes, staffing-sector early-cycle sensitivity, rate-sensitive finance) did real work in this analysis, but I used them to discount the strength of the attribution and wage panels rather than as a named cause resolving a displacement finding, which is the correct place for them under the rules as I understand them.

Overturn design: I chose the reabsorption headline's 12-month change as the primary field because it is the panel that decides reallocation-vs-displacement and it is fresh (2026-07) and will publish again within the window. A single touch of -0.5 already occurred once (2026-06) and reversed, so on its own that threshold is not discriminating — an ordinary noisy month could trip it again without meaning displacement. I therefore required, as the second condition, that the exposed-vs-control jobs differential also reach its own pre-registered alarm line (-2.48, two sigma below the clean 2010-19 baseline) at the same time. Requiring both — aggregate absorption cracking AND the exposed-specific divergence simultaneously reaching alarm — is a much harder bar for noise to clear than either alone, while still being reachable: the differential is currently only 0.13 away from that line and has been in the low -2 range for a while, and the headline has already grazed -0.5 once this year, so neither condition is set beyond the horizon of what these series actually do. Both panels are monthly and will report multiple times before 2026-11-24, so the test can actually fire, not just sit unreachable.

Per the panel's own weighting rule ("if the gap is widening while absorption holds steady, workers are moving rather than being removed"), and given the gap is not clearly widening here, I read this as reallocation-not-yet-displacement, i.e., closer to "displacement not started" than to "displacement observed." I am stating explicitly that this rests mainly on the ABSENCE of deterioration (flat prime-age ratio, low layoffs, hires still ahead of quits) rather than on positive evidence that exposed workers are being made more valuable — so the correct label under the forced choice is AUGMENTATION, but with the caveat foregrounded rather than dressed up as a stronger claim.

exposed_vs_control_wages (as_of 2026-07): exposed pay +4.22% YoY vs control +3.21%, differential +1.00, rising from +0.93. On its face this differential favors exposed workers and could be read as augmentation (AI-adjacent workers commanding a growing premium). But the panel's own measurement_artifact is decisive here: exposed employment is FALLING (-1.19% YoY, per the jobs panel), and the weighting_rule states that when exposed employment is falling, a composition story (junior/lower-paid workers leaving the denominator, pulling the average up with nobody getting a raise) predicts exactly this same observation, so the panel "cannot separate them by itself." I checked the cross-check panel — individual_wage_growth (COMPOSITION_CONTROL, economy-wide, same-people basis): job stayers 3.6%, switchers 4.4%, switcher premium 0.8, essentially at its long-run fixed-baseline average (mean 0.58, sd 0.41 → about 0.5σ) and unchanged from the prior month. This is economy-wide so it cannot itself confirm or deny an exposed-industry story, but it gives no sign of an unusual, broad acceleration in switcher pay that would need to ride alongside a genuine exposed-industry pay story. Given that, I treat the exposed-vs-control wage differential as likely substantially composition-driven and I am NOT counting it as positive evidence for augmentation, consistent with the instruction not to quote an unresolved composition figure at face value. Inversion done: the strongest opposite reading (rising exposed pay = real augmentation) is the one I set aside for the composition reason above, stated in the panel's own terms (falling exposed employment + industry-average mechanics), not by citation of the panel_role label.

job_postings_spread (as_of 2026-08, freshest panel, earliest-moving per its own role): exposed occupations -23 vs own Feb-2020 baseline, control +4.6; spread -27.6, essentially flat vs -27.9 last month, and per its own measurement_artifact this spread opened in 2022 on the back of the tightening cycle (rate-sensitive white-collar hiring cut first), predating diffused AI use in hiring — so the LEVEL is substantially a stale 2022 event and I read only the CHANGE. Six-month change is +4 (spread narrowing, i.e., mild improvement on the exposed side relative to control) and the one-month change is +0.3. Both are small relative to the series' own full-history sd of 4.39, so I treat this as "not currently deteriorating further" rather than "recovering" — a weak, noisy signal that nonetheless does not contradict the reabsorption-based read. Inversion: since postings lead employment, a reader could argue this flatness is exactly the kind of thing that would turn first if a real deterioration were coming, and a single month's +0.3 tells us nothing about whether that turn is imminent — I accept that and it is part of why confidence stays LOW rather than moving up.

labor_productivity (GAINS_TEST, economy-wide, as_of 2026-06 — two months older than the July-dated exposed/reabsorption panels, noted per the vintage rule): 2.2%, down from 2.9%, now below the 2.7 "internet-boom" lower band for one quarter. This is explicitly a check on the AUGMENTATION story rather than on displacement (it's economy-wide and can't attribute to AI either way), and it argues against a strong positive augmentation claim — gains are not visibly accelerating in the aggregate, if anything decelerating. I used this to keep the verdict modest ("displacement not started" rather than "augmentation working") rather than to move it toward displacement, since panel_role explicitly says gains being absent is consistent with several things including simple technological immaturity, and it cannot speak to exposed-industry displacement.

ai_adoption: rising steadily (17.3%→21.8% since Nov 2025), concentrated more in larger firms (41.5% for 250+ vs 21.9% for the smallest band), so worker-level exposure is understated by the firm-count headline. This establishes that the deployment precondition for an AI-labor story is present and growing — it "removes an objection" to an AI-specific explanation existing at all, per its own panel note — but per the same note it carries no firm-level linkage to any layoff and cannot itself supply a labor-market finding. I used it only as background plausibility, not as evidence either way.

worker_share_of_income: economy-wide, declining for 40+ years, currently in the fastest 5% of 4-quarter declines on record, but the panel itself notes that ordinary recessions (2009, 2010) produced faster declines than this, and it explicitly cannot be attributed to AI. I read it as descriptive texture only, consistent with its DESCRIPTIVE role and its own no-threshold registration — a real move, but not specific to AI-exposed work and not usable as attribution.

ai_use_automation_vs_augmentation, ai_capability_metr, ai_capability_gdpval_ratings, ai_capability_vs_human_experts: all either stale (11 and 8 months old) or explicitly does_not_contribute. I read them for texture only — the automation/augmentation split (43/57) has been stable across releases but predates the current labor months by most of a year and is vendor-usage-based, not a labor measure; the capability panels show frontier models continuing to improve on clean benchmark tasks (up to ~186 minutes at 80% reliability, and GPT-5.2 Thinking clearing experts 70.9% of the time wins+ties, 49.7% wins-only i.e. near true parity) but none of that is an event in any worker's employment, so none of it moved the verdict, consistent with their panel_role.

macro_regime (as_of 2026-08): yield curve not inverted (10y-2y = +0.5), real 10yr yield 2.4%, expected inflation 2.3%. I did not use this to exculpate any weakness already in the data (the prompt is explicit the curve is forward-looking and cannot do that). Instead I ran the contemporaneous test the prompt asks for: control industries are growing at +1.16% YoY, i.e., healthy, which argues against a general macro slump being the story behind the exposed-industry softness — that softness looks more specific to the exposed codes than to the economy broadly, though I still can't cleanly separate "AI" from "media strikes / staffing-sector leading indicator / rate-sensitive finance" within those codes, which is exactly why I kept this reading at LOW rather than promoting it to a confident directional call.

News package: BLS ground truth for July shows payrolls -23k (essentially flat) and unemployment 4.1%, consistent with the flat reabsorption headline and not indicating a fresh air-pocket. The two AP wire pieces are generic macro texture (inflation, Iran, Fed, mortgage rates) with no specific mechanism tying them to AI-exposed industries specifically, so I set them aside — they could move rates or general sentiment but nothing in them explains why exposed pay/employment would move differently from control. The NY Fed "stock market participation and rate transmission" piece is about monetary-policy mechanics, not labor displacement, and I set it aside on the same grounds. The NY Fed "AI's Impact on Labor and Hiring" piece is the one on-topic item, but I have only the title, not tested content, and per the rules news generates hypotheses but never moves the verdict — I have nothing in it I can test against a series beyond what the dashboard panels themselves already carry, so it neither strengthens nor weakens my read; I note its existence rather than use it.

Rejected verdict: DISPLACEMENT. The case for it would need either the attribution panel to be escalating (it is not — flat/newly-at-attention rather than accelerating toward alarm) or the reabsorption headline to be deteriorating (it is flat, and its supporting hiring/layoffs legs are improving, not worsening). The strongest displacement-leaning fact — underemployment gap at 1.81σ — is undercut by its own 3-month easing, so I could not treat it as decisive.

Rejected verdict: CONFOUNDED. This is available only when a named cause fully explains an otherwise-displacement-shaped pattern. Here I am not reading a displacement-shaped pattern to begin with — the reabsorption panel that is supposed to decide that question shows no deterioration — so there is no positive displacement reading left for a confounder to explain away. The industry-proxy issues (strikes, staffing-sector early-cycle sensitivity, rate-sensitive finance) did real work in this analysis, but I used them to discount the strength of the attribution and wage panels rather than as a named cause resolving a displacement finding, which is the correct place for them under the rules as I understand them.

Overturn design: I chose the reabsorption headline's 12-month change as the primary field because it is the panel that decides reallocation-vs-displacement and it is fresh (2026-07) and will publish again within the window. A single touch of -0.5 already occurred once (2026-06) and reversed, so on its own that threshold is not discriminating — an ordinary noisy month could trip it again without meaning displacement. I therefore required, as the second condition, that the exposed-vs-control jobs differential also reach its own pre-registered alarm line (-2.48, two sigma below the clean 2010-19 baseline) at the same time. Requiring both — aggregate absorption cracking AND the exposed-specific divergence simultaneously reaching alarm — is a much harder bar for noise to clear than either alone, while still being reachable: the differential is currently only 0.13 away from that line and has been in the low -2 range for a while, and the headline has already grazed -0.5 once this year, so neither condition is set beyond the horizon of what these series actually do. Both panels are monthly and will report multiple times before 2026-11-24, so the test can actually fire, not just sit unreachable.

pass2.publishedNote:
The augmentation reading holds this month: the data still show industries most exposed to AI reallocating workers rather than shedding them en masse. That conclusion rests on the absence of deterioration in the numbers that would show displacement, not on positive proof that AI is making these workers more productive — worth stating plainly, since it is the whole basis for the call.

What's new since last month is minor and sits outside the panels that decide the call. The postings gap between AI-exposed and less-exposed occupations narrowed slightly, from -27.9 to -27.6, inside normal month-to-month noise. The worker share of national income fell further, now among the fastest declines in decades, but that is an economy-wide figure unrelated specifically to AI-exposed industries, and the update reflects newly available older data rather than a fresh one-month move. A benchmark of AI capability against human experts dipped slightly, which measures what AI can do, not what has happened to any worker's job.

The strongest support for the augmentation reading: the measure that tracks whether people leaving AI-exposed work land somewhere else shows no trouble. Employment among prime-working-age adults is exactly flat over the past year and sits above its pre-pandemic level. Layoffs are not elevated, and companies are still hiring faster than people are quitting. If a real wave of AI-driven displacement were underway, this is where it would show up first, and it isn't.

The strongest thing arguing against it: AI-exposed industries are still losing jobs while other industries keep growing. Employment in exposed industries fell 1.19% over the past year while the comparison group grew 1.16%, and that gap has held at roughly this size for four straight months without closing. It also just crossed a line the analysis treats as historically unusual, even though it improved slightly from the prior month. That is a real tension: a gap that is both newly abnormal and not accelerating is a plateau, not a resolution, and should not be read as reassuring. A broader underemployment measure sits close to the same unusual territory, though its recent trend is easing rather than worsening — ambiguous, not a clean confirmation either way. Separately, exposed-industry pay is growing faster than the comparison group's, 4.2% against 3.2%, which looks like good news for those workers, but exposed-industry employment is shrinking at the same time — when lower-paid workers leave a shrinking group first, the average pay of who remains rises for arithmetic reasons, with nobody actually getting a raise. That gap was not counted as evidence of augmentation.

What to watch: the employment rate for prime-working-age adults is the single number that would move first if this plateau tips into real displacement.
pass2.fullAnalysis:
The augmentation reading holds this month. That means the data still support a story of AI-exposed workers being reallocated rather than displaced en masse — but that conclusion rests almost entirely on the absence of deterioration in the numbers that would show displacement, not on positive proof that AI is making exposed workers more valuable. That distinction matters and is worth keeping in view through everything below.

What changed since last month: very little, and nothing in the panels that actually decide the call. Three numbers moved. The postings gap between AI-exposed occupations and a control group of less-exposed occupations narrowed slightly, from -27.9 to -27.6 — a change of 0.3, well inside the normal month-to-month noise of a series that has moved in a range of roughly plus or minus 4 points historically. The worker share of national income fell further, to a level now among the fastest declines of the last several decades, but this is an economy-wide figure that says nothing specific about AI-exposed industries, and the update itself reflects three additional months of data becoming available, not a fresh one-month move. And a benchmark comparing AI model output to human expert ratings dipped slightly (-13.8 on its scale), which is a measure of what AI can do, not a measure of what has happened to any worker's job, so it does not bear on the labor-market call either way. None of these three are the panels the verdict is built on.

The panel that decides the call is the one tracking whether people who leave AI-exposed work are landing somewhere else. The clearest sign of trouble would be a falling employment rate among prime-working-age adults. That rate is exactly flat over the past year, and it sits above its own pre-pandemic level. Two supporting figures back this up: layoffs are not elevated relative to their own history, and companies are still hiring people faster than existing employees are quitting, which rules out the "employers have simply stopped hiring" version of a displacement story. If a wave of AI-driven job loss were underway and unresolved, this is where it would first become visible in the data, and right now it is not visible.

Set against that is a genuine, unresolved tension. Employment in AI-exposed industries fell 1.19% over the past year, while employment in the comparison group of less-exposed industries rose 1.16% over the same period — exposed industries are shrinking, non-exposed industries are growing, and that gap has held at roughly this size for four straight monthly readings without closing. This month the gap also crossed a line the analysis treats as historically unusual for the first time, even though the gap itself improved slightly compared to the prior month (it had been wider, at -2.57, the month before). Both things are true at once: a newly-unusual gap, and a gap that is not accelerating. That combination should not be read as either good news or bad news resolving itself — it is a plateau at an already-abnormal level, and plateaus can tip in either direction. It is not evidence the divergence is closing.

A second soft spot sits alongside this. A broader measure of underemployment — people working part-time who would rather work full-time, measured against the plain unemployment rate — is close to the same historically unusual territory the exposed-jobs gap just crossed. But this measure's own three-month trend has been easing, not worsening, which disagrees with the twelve-month trend pointing the other way. I read this as genuinely ambiguous rather than as confirming the exposed-jobs signal, but it is not a clean reassurance either.

One number looks, on its face, like direct evidence for augmentation and was deliberately not counted as such. Pay in AI-exposed industries grew 4.2% over the past year against 3.2% in the comparison group — exposed workers' pay pulling ahead. But exposed-industry employment is shrinking at the same time, and when a shrinking group loses its lower-paid workers first, the average pay of whoever remains rises automatically, with nobody actually getting a raise. A separate, economy-wide measure of individual pay growth (tracking the same people over time, not an industry average) shows switchers earning about 0.8 points more than people who stay in their jobs — squarely at its own long-run average, with no sign of an unusual acceleration that would need to accompany a genuine exposed-industry pay story. Because of this, the pay gap was treated as most likely a composition effect, not counted as support for augmentation. This is the same reason a raw productivity figure was not used to argue augmentation is accelerating: economy-wide productivity growth actually slowed to 2.2% from 2.9%, below the pace associated with previous technology-driven productivity booms, and because it is an economy-wide number it cannot be attributed to AI-exposed work specifically either way — it was used only to keep the overall confidence modest, not to move the verdict toward displacement.

Two alternative verdicts were considered and set aside. A displacement verdict would require either the exposed-industry jobs gap to be actively widening, or the reabsorption measure to be deteriorating; neither is happening this month. A confounded verdict — some named, non-AI cause fully explaining an otherwise displacement-shaped pattern — was not available because there is no displacement-shaped pattern to explain in the first place: the reabsorption panel that would need to show deterioration for a confounder to be relevant instead shows none. Factors like entertainment-industry strikes and staffing-sector cyclicality that show up inside the "exposed industries" grouping were used to discount how much weight the jobs and wage gaps deserve, rather than as a confounder resolving a finding that isn't there.

Background context worth naming without over-weighting: AI adoption among firms continues to climb steadily (roughly 17% to 22% of firms since late 2025), concentrated more heavily at large firms, which establishes that the underlying technology is being deployed at meaningfully greater scale — a plausibility check, not itself a labor-market finding. The bond market shows no inversion and stable inflation expectations, arguing against a general economic slump explaining the exposed-industry softness, though this cannot rule out a slowdown specific to a few subsectors within the "exposed" grouping. A wire report on AI's impact on hiring exists in this month's news but was not tested against any specific figure in this analysis and did not move the reading either direction.

falsifier.unit: percentage points (12-month change in prime-age 25-54 employment-population ratio)

runs.falsifierPlain: This reading is wrong if the reabsorption panel's headline prime-age employment ratio falls to a 12-month change of -0.5 points or worse (from 0 now) while exposed-vs-control control-industry job growth stays at or above +0.5% year-over-year, showing exposed workers failing to land even though the rest of the economy is not in a general slump.

pairedState.reading: AI-exposed work is diverging AND the aggregate is deteriorating, so the outflow is not landing.

definitions.widening: the exposed-minus-control job-growth gap is at least 0 standard deviation further below its 2010-01..2019-12 average, that window fixed and never rolling, AND has been for 3 consecutive readings. The run requirement is the newer half and it is what stops the vertical axis deciding this grid on its own: one month past the line used to establish this axis, the gap has been past the line since 2023, and the result was that the only thing ever changing the quadrant was an economy-wide employment change that an ordinary recession moves
definitions.deteriorating: the prime-age (25-54) employment-population ratio is LOWER than it was twelve months ago. A change against raw zero, with no baseline, no reference year and no threshold, because those were all the wrong kind of answer here: a level against 2019 anchored the boundary to a cyclical peak and would have read displacement across most of the 2010s, and z-scoring the change against 2010-2019 scored a mature expansion against a decade of recovery. Zero involves no distribution, so nothing can contaminate it.

runs.computedDissent: The analyst read AUGMENTATION from the panels without being shown either mechanical reading, and the four-corner grid places this month at DISPLACEMENT (gap wide and holding, aggregate deteriorating). Recorded, not resolved: these are different routes through the same data, and neither one overrules the other. The grid in particular turns on a single economy-wide series sitting near zero, so a month's disagreement with it is ordinary rather than a mark against either reading.

pass1.confidenceBasis: Corroborating: reabsorption headline (flat 12m change, the decisive readout per its own binding rule) and control-industry job growth (+1.16% YoY, exposed_vs_control_jobs) showing the exposed-industry contraction is not a general downturn. Weakening/unresolved: the underemployment gap secondary readout (deviation 1.81 against its fixed baseline, alarm at 2, rising) and the 3-month fast-horizon on the reabsorption headline itself (falling -0.3, deviation 1.95, context-only but close to alarm) are both leading indicators pointing the other way and are not yet resolved by the binding 12-month figure. The doubt "is anything that leads this pointing the other way" is answered mixed: job postings (the earliest mover) show slight narrowing (+4 over 6 months), agreeing with this verdict, while the reabsorption fast-horizon disagrees. This is a directional read that barely clears the bar, not a coherent multi-panel story.

falsifier.unit: percentage points (12-month change in prime-age 25-54 employment-population ratio)

pass1.falsifierPlain: This reading is wrong if the reabsorption panel's headline prime-age employment ratio falls to a 12-month change of -0.5 points or worse (from 0 now) while exposed-vs-control control-industry job growth stays at or above +0.5% year-over-year, showing exposed workers failing to land even though the rest of the economy is not in a general slump.
pass1.reasoningLog:
STARTING POINT — what each ATTRIBUTION-class panel actually shows, naming the moving side.

exposed_vs_control_jobs (as_of 2026-07, 1 month old): exposed industries employment is DOWN 1.19% YoY (an absolute contraction, not just slower growth); control industries are UP 1.16% YoY. The differential (-2.35) sits past its attention line (deviation 1.82 against the preferred fixed 2010-2019 baseline, alarm at 2) and has been "holding roughly flat over the last 4 readings" — so this is a real, sustained, specific-to-exposed-industry divergence, not a one-month blip. Per the panel's own measurement_artifact, this is explicitly consistent with EITHER mass displacement or perfect reallocation ("100 jobs eliminated, 100 workers land in construction/health care" produces the maximally negative reading on this panel with nobody left behind). It cannot be read alone. I use it only to establish that something specific is happening to AI-exposed work, and I take the panel's own weighting rule at face value: go to reabsorption before concluding anything.

Contemporaneous macro test (per the yield-curve instruction): macro_regime shows the curve is NOT inverted (10y-2y = +0.5), and — more importantly, since curves are forward-looking and cannot clear weakness already in the data — the CONTROL industries in exposed_vs_control_jobs are themselves growing at +1.16% YoY, i.e., healthy. A general downturn would drag construction, leisure/hospitality and education/health down too; it hasn't.
