The reading is augmentation, and nothing has moved since last month — this is the same call, on the same evidence, for a second month running.

That call rests on an absence of deterioration, not on any positive sign that AI is making workers more productive. The prime-age employment rate, which tracks whether adults are working at all regardless of industry, has been flat over the past year. Long-term unemployment is only mildly up, and hiring relative to quits is actually improving. That is the strongest thing behind the verdict: whatever is happening to exposed-industry jobs, the broader labor market is currently catching the fallout rather than failing to.

The strongest thing against it is that exposed-industry employment is actually shrinking — down 1.19% over the past year — while employment in industries AI barely touches, like construction and health care, is growing 1.16%. That gap has now sat in roughly the same place for four straight months without closing. On top of that, a broader measure of underemployment is edging up, and the reabsorption measure's own faster three-month reading is falling toward concerning territory well ahead of the slower twelve-month figure this whole call depends on. If that faster decline continues for another couple of months, the flat twelve-month reading behind this verdict could turn negative.

Two things looked like evidence but are not being counted as such. Pay is growing faster in exposed industries than in others, but exposed-industry employment is shrinking at the same time, so that faster pay growth could simply reflect fewer, more senior workers left in the average rather than anyone getting genuinely more valuable. And a broader productivity measure, where real augmentation should eventually show up economy-wide, actually eased this quarter rather than picking up.

What to watch: the reabsorption panel's headline prime-age employment measure, and specifically whether its faster three-month reading keeps sliding — that is the number that would move first if this reading is about to turn.
pass2.fullAnalysis:
The reading is augmentation, and it has not changed since last month. Two small panels ticked slightly — the share of firms using AI in any business function edged up to 22.4% from 21.8%, and a measure of how AI systems perform against human experts on rated tasks dipped a fraction — but neither of these speaks to what has actually happened to a worker, and neither moves the verdict. Every panel that does bear on the verdict is unchanged from last month.

Start with what the verdict rests on. Employment in AI-exposed industries is down 1.19% over the past year — an actual contraction, not merely slower growth — while employment in industries AI barely touches (construction, health care, leisure and hospitality) is up 1.16% over the same period. That gap has now held in roughly the same place for four consecutive months. On its own, this kind of divergence cannot distinguish two very different stories: workers being pushed out of exposed industries with nowhere to go, versus workers moving out of exposed industries into growing ones. A survey of employment by industry cannot tell you where the people who left exposed industries ended up.

That is exactly the question the reabsorption measure is built to answer, and this month, as last month, its answer is that the broader labor market is absorbing whatever churn is happening upstream. The prime-age employment rate — the share of 25-to-54-year-olds actually working, which does not care what industry someone works in, only whether they are employed at all — is unchanged over the past twelve months. Long-term unemployment is only mildly elevated. Hiring relative to quits is actually improving, and layoffs are falling. None of that looks like an economy failing to catch people who lost exposed-industry jobs. It looks, plainly, like an absence of deterioration rather than positive evidence that AI is making workers more productive or valuable — the augmentation reading right now is a story about what has not happened, not about gains that have shown up. Economy-wide productivity growth, which is where you would expect to see augmentation's fingerprints if it were real and material, actually eased this quarter (2.2%, down from 2.9%) rather than accelerating.

The strongest thing arguing against this reading is the persistence itself. A four-month-old, unmoving gap between falling exposed-industry employment and rising control-industry employment is not a blip — it is a standing feature of the data that an augmentation story has to explain, and simply pointing to a healthy aggregate labor market does not make it disappear. Two additional pieces of the reabsorption picture, while not the deciding factor by the panel's own logic, point the same direction: the gap between the official unemployment rate and a broader measure that includes underemployed workers is widening, hinting that some of the people leaving exposed industries may be landing in worse jobs even while staying employed. And the reabsorption measure's own faster three-month reading is falling, sitting close to the point that would flag concern, well ahead of the slower twelve-month figure that currently reads flat. If that faster reading keeps falling for another two or three months, the twelve-month figure this whole call rests on could very plausibly turn negative.

Two other panels deserve honest treatment rather than being folded silently into the case for augmentation. Pay in exposed industries is growing faster than in control industries (4.2% versus 3.2% year over year), which looks like a wage-based augmentation signal at first glance — but exposed-industry employment is simultaneously shrinking, and a shrinking, more-senior workforce can push average pay up mechanically even if nobody individually got a raise. This panel cannot distinguish those stories, so it is not being counted as evidence either way. Separately, hiring demand for knowledge-work occupations sits about a quarter below where it stood before COVID, while hiring demand for hands-on occupations sits modestly above its own pre-COVID level. That gap has narrowed slightly over the past six months, a mild positive, but a reader could just as easily argue the multi-year depth of that gap shows demand destruction that already happened and has merely stopped getting worse, rather than a market that is healing.

No specific alternative explanation — a strike, a merger wave, a rate-driven slump in a particular industry — is supported in this month's data as the actual driver of the exposed-industry contraction, so this is not being called a confounded reading. But the absence of a named alternative cause is not the same as confidence in the AI explanation; it means the direction is read as it stands, at low confidence, resting mainly on the fact that the aggregate labor market has not yet shown signs of failing to catch people.

Economy-wide productivity growth, which is where you would expect to see augmentation's fingerprints if it were real and material, actually eased this quarter (2.2%, down from 2.9%) rather than accelerating.

The strongest thing arguing against this reading is the persistence itself. A four-month-old, unmoving gap between falling exposed-industry employment and rising control-industry employment is not a blip — it is a standing feature of the data that an augmentation story has to explain, and simply pointing to a healthy aggregate labor market does not make it disappear. Two additional pieces of the reabsorption picture, while not the deciding factor by the panel's own logic, point the same direction: the gap between the official unemployment rate and a broader measure that includes underemployed workers is widening, hinting that some of the people leaving exposed industries may be landing in worse jobs even while staying employed. And the reabsorption measure's own faster three-month reading is falling, sitting close to the point that would flag concern, well ahead of the slower twelve-month figure that currently reads flat. If that faster reading keeps falling for another two or three months, the twelve-month figure this whole call rests on could very plausibly turn negative.

Two other panels deserve honest treatment rather than being folded silently into the case for augmentation. Pay in exposed industries is growing faster than in control industries (4.2% versus 3.2% year over year), which looks like a wage-based augmentation signal at first glance — but exposed-industry employment is simultaneously shrinking, and a shrinking, more-senior workforce can push average pay up mechanically even if nobody individually got a raise. This panel cannot distinguish those stories, so it is not being counted as evidence either way. Separately, hiring demand for knowledge-work occupations sits about a quarter below where it stood before COVID, while hiring demand for hands-on occupations sits modestly above its own pre-COVID level. That gap has narrowed slightly over the past six months, a mild positive, but a reader could just as easily argue the multi-year depth of that gap shows demand destruction that already happened and has merely stopped getting worse, rather than a market that is healing.

No specific alternative explanation — a strike, a merger wave, a rate-driven slump in a particular industry — is supported in this month's data as the actual driver of the exposed-industry contraction, so this is not being called a confounded reading. But the absence of a named alternative cause is not the same as confidence in the AI explanation; it means the direction is read as it stands, at low confidence, resting mainly on the fact that the aggregate labor market has not yet shown signs of failing to catch people.

PUBLISHED_NOTE:
The reading is augmentation, and nothing has moved since last month — this is the same call, on the same evidence, for a second month running.

That call rests on an absence of deterioration, not on any positive sign that AI is making workers more productive. The prime-age employment rate, which tracks whether adults are working at all regardless of industry, has been flat over the past year. Long-term unemployment is only mildly up, and hiring relative to quits is actually improving. That is the strongest thing behind the verdict: whatever is happening to exposed-industry jobs, the broader labor market is currently catching the fallout rather than failing to.

The strongest thing against it is that exposed-industry employment is actually shrinking — down 1.19% over the past year — while employment in industries AI barely touches, like construction and health care, is growing 1.16%. That gap has now sat in roughly the same place for four straight months without closing. On top of that, a broader measure of underemployment is edging up, and the reabsorption measure's own faster three-month reading is falling toward concerning territory well ahead of the slower twelve-month figure this whole call depends on. If that faster decline continues for another couple of months, the flat twelve-month reading behind this verdict could turn negative.

Two things looked like evidence but are not being counted as such. Pay is growing faster in exposed industries than in others, but exposed-industry employment is shrinking at the same time, so that faster pay growth could simply reflect fewer, more senior workers left in the average rather than anyone getting genuinely more valuable. And a broader productivity measure, where real augmentation should eventually show up economy-wide, actually eased this quarter rather than picking up.

What to watch: the reabsorption panel's headline prime-age employment measure, and specifically whether its faster three-month reading keeps sliding — that is the number that would move first if this reading is about to turn.

pass1.reasoningLog:
FRAMING: This reads as "displacement not started," not "augmentation working." I have no positive evidence that AI-exposed workers are being made more valuable — productivity growth (the one panel built to test that) is decelerating (2.9%→2.2%, dropping below the 2.7 "boom" band), and the wage evidence in favor is confounded. What I actually have is: an elevated but non-worsening attribution signal, sitting beside an absorption headline that is not deteriorating. That is an absence-of-deterioration case, and I am saying so plainly rather than dressing it as augmentation succeeding.

PANEL BY PANEL:

exposed_vs_control_jobs (as_of 2026-07, 2mo old). Differential -2.35, deviation 1.82 against the preferred fixed pre-2020 baseline (attention line 1, alarm line 2) — past attention, short of alarm, "holding roughly flat over the last 4 readings," and actually improved slightly from -2.57 last month. The panel's own artifact block is explicit that this measures reallocation, not destruction: perfect reallocation with everyone re-employed produces the maximally negative reading here, same as mass displacement would. So on its own this establishes only that something is specific to exposed work (industry-proxy caveats duly noted — "information" includes publishing/broadcasting hit by old strike effects, "professional/business services" includes temp staffing that leads any slowdown). INVERSION: a gap parked past attention for 4 straight months could equally be read as steady-state ongoing displacement that just hasn't cascaded into the (lagging, noisy) aggregate absorption numbers yet — flatness is compatible with either "reallocation has stabilized" or "displacement is proceeding at a constant, unremarkable pace." I cannot resolve that from this panel alone, which is exactly why the reabsorption panel is the tiebreaker per its own weighting rule.

reabsorption (as_of 2026-07, 2mo old). Headline (LNS12300060) 12-month change = 0, flat, and per its own reading_rule this is the field that binds; the four secondary readouts and the 3-month fast_horizon are explicitly context, not votes. Level: 0.45 points ABOVE the 2019 reference — still historically strong. Secondary readouts: long-term unemployed share rising mildly (deviation 0.31, below attention); hires-minus-quits flat 12m (deviation -0.07, essentially normal) though its 3-month leg is softening; layoffs_rate falling and BELOW norm (deviation -0.34) — layoffs are not elevated, so this is not a shedding/cyclical contraction. Per the panel's own reading_rule_with_hires, weak hiring alongside low layoffs is a FROZEN market, where the burden falls on entrants rather than incumbents — that is a real caveat on my reading: "absorption holding" here mainly means existing workers aren't being pushed out, not that switchers/new entrants are landing well. Underemployment gap (U6-U3) is the one secondary readout that worries me: deviation 1.81 against the fixed baseline, close to its alarm line, rising 12m (+0.2), though its 3-month leg is improving (-0.1). INVERSION: the headline's own 3-month fast_horizon is -0.3 with deviation 1.95 (near alarm) and explicitly disagrees with the flat 12-month figure ("agrees_with_headline": false). A 12-month change is slow by construction; if the recent monthly weakness that produced that -0.3 continues, the flat headline will itself go negative within a couple of prints. I am knowingly citing the slower, currently-more-reassuring number over the faster one, and I say so rather than hide it.

exposed_vs_control_wages (as_of 2026-07, 2mo old). Differential +1.0, widened from +0.93, deviation -0.6 (orientation: negative moves AWAY from displacement, since the panel's alarm is exposed pay falling below control, not exceeding it). On its face this looks supportive of an augmentation/no-harm read: exposed pay is growing faster than control. But the panel's own weighting_rule is decisive here: exposed employment is FALLING (-1.19% YoY, confirmed on the jobs panel), and when exposed employment is falling, a composition story (juniors/lower-paid leaving the denominator) and a genuine wage story predict the identical observation — this panel cannot separate them. The cross-check, individual_wage_growth (economy-wide, follows the same people 12 months apart), shows the switcher premium flat at 0.8, actually BELOW its own historical average (deviation -0.54) — no sign of an accelerating bidding war for movers. That does not corroborate a genuine exposed-industry wage-acceleration story, so I am treating exposed_vs_control_wages as neutralized rather than as support: it neither strengthens nor contradicts my verdict, and I am not using its face-value number.

job_postings_spread (as_of 2026-08, 1mo old — the freshest panel here). Exposed postings sit 23% below their own Feb-2020 level; control sits 4.6% above. Naming the moving side: it is overwhelmingly the exposed side that is depressed, not the control side that is elevated. The spread has been roughly flat since 2022 and the panel's own artifact block attributes much of the original opening to the 2022 rate-tightening cycle hitting rate-sensitive white-collar hiring, not to AI diffusion, which postdates the opening. The one live datum is spread_change_over_6_months = +4 (narrowing, i.e., moving toward parity), which is a mild point against fresh deterioration, though I can't decompose which side moved to produce that narrowing from what's given. INVERSION: a still-deeply-depressed level even with a marginal 6-month narrowing is also consistent with ongoing, unresolved weakness in demand for exposed occupational categories — narrowing off a very low base is a weak signal either way, and I'm not leaning hard on it.

labor_productivity (as_of 2026-06, 3mo old, GAINS_TEST, economy-wide). 2.2% YoY, down from 2.9%, first quarter below the 2.7 lower band line. This is the panel built to show augmentation gains showing up in the aggregate, and it is decelerating, not accelerating. I am not citing this as support for AUGMENTATION — if anything it argues the positive "augmentation working" story is currently NOT visible, which is exactly why I am framing my verdict as "displacement not started" rather than "augmentation confirmed."

CONTEMPORANEOUS MACRO TEST (per the instruction to run it explicitly): macro_regime (as_of 2026-08) shows the yield curve NOT inverted (10yr-2yr = +0.4), real 10yr yield 2.4%, expected inflation 2.3% — the bond market is not pricing an imminent recession, though per the panel's own role note the curve cannot exculpate weakness already in the data; it is forward-looking only. The decisive test is the control industries: control_value on exposed_vs_control_jobs is +1.16% YoY, well above its own fixed pre-2020 mean of -0.99% — controls are running ABOVE their historical norm, not weak. This argues against a general macro slowdown explaining the exposed-industry softness, and supports treating the exposed-industry weakness as something specific to exposed work (consistent with either reallocation or displacement, but not with "it's just the business cycle").

CONFOUNDER CONSIDERED AND SET ASIDE: the panel notes flag that "professional and business services" includes temp-help/staffing, a leading indicator that turns early in ANY slowdown, and that the 2023 writers'/actors' strikes fall inside "information." Both are genuine candidate confounders for the exposed-industry composition, but I have no separate temp-help or entertainment-strike series in this payload to point to as supporting evidence for a magnitude estimate, and the strikes are two years stale relative to the current 2026-07 reading, so I cannot invoke CONFOUNDED formally (the rule requires naming a specific competing cause AND pointing to a supporting series in the payload). I note it as an interpretive caveat on the industry-proxy quality of the attribution panels, not as a formal confounder finding.

NEWS CONSIDERED AND SET ASIDE: BLS ground truth (-23k payrolls, 4.1% unemployment) is economy-wide and one month; it doesn't speak to the exposed-vs-control split and I am not pairing it with the exposed-industry figures per the rule against mixing populations. AP wire texture pieces (inflation, Iran, tariffs, Fed, mortgage) could plausibly move energy costs, rate expectations, or general hiring sentiment, but nothing in them explains why the exposed-industry jobs differential specifically sits past its attention line while control industries run above their historical average — a general-condition story should hit both legs, and it isn't. The NY Fed "AI's Impact on Labor and Hiring" piece is exactly on-topic, but I only have its headline in the allowlist, not its findings, and per the instructions a remembered or half-known conclusion is not evidence — I am not importing anything from it beyond noting that outside researchers are asking the same question this dashboard asks; it does not move the verdict, series do.

CROSS-PANEL VINTAGE CHECK: exposed_vs_control_jobs and reabsorption are both as_of 2026-07 (2 months old) — comparable, no gap to flag. job_postings_spread is one month fresher (2026-08). labor_productivity is 3 months old (2026-06) and is the oldest panel I discuss; since it argues mildly AGAINST my own verdict (deceleration, no augmentation gains visible) and is older than the panels supporting my read, I am noting explicitly that this counter-leaning evidence is not fresher than my supporting evidence — it does not get to be dismissed as stale-therefore-wrong, but it also doesn't get to trump the two-months-fresher reabsorption/attribution pair on recency grounds either way.

WHY LOW AND NOT MEDIUM: (1) Persistence — the attribution signal (exposed_vs_control_jobs past attention line) has held for 4 readings, which is real, not a single-month artifact; but the absorption side's reassuring reading rests heavily on the household survey (prime-age ratio, long-term unemployment share, underemployment gap are all CPS-based) — three of four reabsorption readouts share one data source, which is weaker corroboration than it looks, per the dashboard's own warning. (2) Genuinely different source agreement — JOLTS-based layoffs_rate (a different survey) does agree (low, not elevated), which helps, but it's a single independent corroborator against three same-source readouts. (3) Leading indicator check — the reabsorption headline's own 3-month fast_horizon and the underemployment gap both lean softer than the bound 12-month figure I am citing, which is the specific unmet doubt: something that would normally move first is pointing the other way. Given that unmet doubt and the confounded wage panel, LOW is the honest rating; I would not be surprised if the next reading or two flips this toward displacement.

pass2.publishedNote:
The augmentation verdict holds this month: there is still no sign that AI is displacing workers faster than the economy can absorb them. That reading rests mainly on an absence of deterioration, not on positive proof that AI is making exposed workers more productive — worth saying plainly, because it changes how much weight the verdict can bear.

What's new is almost nothing. Since last month, a broad financial-conditions measure eased slightly (0.5 to 0.4) and an AI-capability benchmark ticked up two points (1822 to 1824). Neither matters. Every other panel behind this call — jobs, wages, absorption, productivity — carries the same figures it carried last month.

The strongest support: the share of prime-age adults (25-54) who are employed was flat over the past year and sits above its pre-pandemic level, while layoffs are running below their historical norm — people already in jobs are not being pushed out. The weakness that exists is concentrated specifically in AI-exposed industries: hiring in industries AI barely touches is running well above its own historical pace, so a general economic slowdown doesn't explain what's happening in exposed industries.

The strongest thing against it is two-sided. First, the flat employment figure above is a 12-month number, which moves slowly; the same measure's faster 3-month reading is already pointing down and disagrees with the flat headline — something that would move first is already leaning the other way, it just hasn't dragged the slower number down yet. Second, and more direct: economy-wide productivity growth — the number that would show AI-driven gains actually showing up — has been decelerating, not accelerating, slipping from 2.9% to 2.2% over the past year, the slowest pace of this stretch.
